Sumiran Devotion Networks: the sankalp that the store called content

Jaipur, Thursday night, 15 October 2026

1. The night before the call

The generator in the lane behind Sumiran Devotion Networks' office on Tonk Road had been running since eight, and Sarayu Vaidyanathan had stopped hearing it. A notice dated 30 September, from the app-review team of one of the two large stores, gave Sumiran until Friday, 30 October to route its Digital Sankalp product through in-app purchase or remove it. Beside it sat a spreadsheet from her data scientist in Toronto, suggesting that the store-search traffic Sumiran had treated as free for four years was traffic it was partly paying for twice.

Digital Sankalp — a devotee books a puja at a partner temple, a pandit performs it at the named hour, and the rite is streamed to her phone with no parcel dispatched — had been sold since February 2024 as a real-world service, billed on Sumiran's rails at a two per cent gateway fee. The reviewer's position took three sentences: a stream with nothing physical attached is digital content, and digital content sold in an app is billed at thirty per cent.

At ten next morning she had forty-five minutes with the review team's India representative, and had not decided what she wanted from it. Diwali fell on 8 November; the board met on 2 November to release a Series B tranche whose conditions she had negotiated in April.

2. How Sumiran got here

Sarayu had spent five years at a Jaipur payments firm before starting Sumiran in June 2019, on the observation that her mother would drive ninety minutes to a temple she trusted rather than switch to the one ten minutes away. The first app, in November 2020, carried a free panchang and advertising. Money arrived with Punya coins in August 2021, a consumable currency spent per minute on live consultations; prasad delivery followed in October 2023 with a courier partner, Sthir Fulfilment Services, and Digital Sankalp in February 2024.

One decision from March 2023 shapes everything available tonight. To lock up supply against better-funded rivals, Sumiran signed three-year panel agreements, negotiated collectively through an astrologers' association called Jyotish Sangam, guaranteeing its 1,400 astrologers forty per cent of gross coin billings, computed before any store commission. Temple agreements from the same quarter give partner trusts sixty-five per cent of booking value, with a most-favoured-nation clause and a bar on charging the devotee a separate platform fee. Both run to 31 March 2027. Supply cost is a fixed share of the number the devotee sees, so every rupee the store takes comes out of Sumiran's share.

3. The market Sumiran sits in

AstroTalk and InstaAstro built per-minute consultation businesses at scale, AstroSage held the kundli ground, Sri Mandir and Vama built temple-side darshan, chadhava and prasad offerings. None competes with Sumiran across coins, subscription and temple services at once, which is its differentiation and its exposure: its revenue straddles the line between digital content and real-world service, where store policy is least settled.

The regulatory surround is thick. The Competition Commission of India's proceedings on Play billing are read inside Sumiran as evidence that the fee question here is live rather than closed, and PhonePe's Indus Appstore has courted Indian developers since 2024 with a lower commission. Under the DPDP Act, 2023 a devotee's birth details are personal data held on consent, and store billing means Sumiran often does not hold the payer's email at all. UPI Autopay works for the ₹200 subscription and not for a devotee in Chicago, whose card renews reliably only when the store bills it. A third of Digital Sankalp orders come from outside India, a diaspora that pays more and cannot receive prasad, since food parcels to the Gulf clear customs unpredictably. The most valuable version of the product is the version with nothing physical in it.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

In February 2024, before launch, Vikram Jhala's legal note called the classification “defensible, on the reading that the devotee is buying a rite performed by a human being at a named temple, of which the stream is only evidence,” and recommended seeking a written interpretation from both stores. Nobody did, and for thirty-one months nothing contradicted it. On 12 August a founder in a WhatsApp group told Sarayu a competitor's livestream product had been reclassified and pulled; it has since emerged that the competitor shipped a couriered tulsi mala with every booking, which makes the comparison worthless either way.

On 26 September build 8.2 moved the booking flow to a web view. Margin per order improved. One-star reviews, 186 of 8,860 India reviews in the preceding nineteen days, became 1,074 of 9,420, or 11.40 per cent, and 612 of those 1,074 — fifty-seven per cent — mentioned payment; the displayed India rating fell from 4.6 to 4.2 and the rank for “online astrologer” slipped from 6 to 9 on a tool that calls such movements indicative only. Vandana Joglekar holds the redirect caused this; Svenja Vollmer holds the redirect was fine and the page it landed on was not.

The notice arrived four days later; Sumiran filed for clarification on 6 October and was given no response window. On 13 October Shalaka Vengsarkar reported that the largest partner trust, the Jankund Devasthan Trust, reads the MFN clause as attaching to gross booking value, so any price rise lifts the trust's take in step, and that Jyotish Sangam has told her fixed payouts reopen the whole panel agreement. Three September beliefs have not survived the month: that the classification was settled; that store search was demand received free; and that the August precedent meant anything.

5. The people

Sarayu Vaidyanathan, founder and chief executive, Jaipur. Wants nothing that risks the listing before Diwali. Not saying: she suspects the app itself, not the store's cut, is what she got wrong.

Jaideep Sirohi, chief technology officer, Pune. Split the SKU: free stream, paid ₹1,018 consignment with a sankalp slot. Not saying: he thinks it reads as circumvention and survives one review cycle.

Vandana Joglekar, head of growth and store optimisation, Hyderabad. Comply at once; her target is installs and keyword rank, not who bills. Not saying: her model books an install to store search whenever no click matches.

Shalaka Vengsarkar, astrologer and temple supply, Varanasi. No price rise, nothing that reopens March 2023 early; she is judged on panel retention while two rivals recruit from her panel. Not saying: the Sangam has asked whether the store's fee will be passed to astrologers.

Vikram Jhala, general counsel, New Delhi. Comply on the record, appeal in parallel; he wrote the ignored 2024 note. Not saying: the strongest position is the one Sumiran cannot afford — in-app purchase plus higher prices, which nobody can call avoidance.

Svenja Vollmer, principal designer, Berlin. The argument over rails has crowded out why a devotee in Nashik abandons the flow at the gotra field. Not saying: she has prototyped a web-first flow making the app optional.

Vineeta Jhaveri, lead data scientist, Toronto. Before deciding what to pay the store, know what it delivers. Not saying: her holdback ran during Pitru Paksha, when demand is suppressed, an effect she cannot separate from the one she claims.

Jatin Vora, international revenue, Chicago. Do not touch overseas billing; store billing is why a diaspora card renews. Not saying: 42.26 per cent of Digital Sankalp revenue is his, the line with most to lose and the one that cannot move to prasad.

8. The options, as Sarayu currently frames them

One: comply fully. Move Digital Sankalp into in-app purchase before 30 October at today's price: the SKU's margin falls from 33.00 per cent to 5.00 per cent. Retained revenue falls from ₹488.96 lakh to ₹456.37 lakh on unchanged volume, which is 34.75 per cent of gross billings against a covenant floor of 36 per cent.

Two: comply and reprice. Raise the price forty per cent to ₹1,018 and take scenario C's volume loss, holding ₹24.55 lakh of the ₹38.41 lakh — but only if the temple payout converts to a fixed amount per booking, which the Jankund trust reads its MFN clause as forbidding and Shalaka will not raise before March.

Three: restructure the SKU. Jaideep's split: free stream, paid consignment. Preserves the Indian economics, reaches none of the 4,800 overseas orders carrying ₹49.19 lakh, and invites the judgement that Sumiran engineered around a ruling four weeks after receiving it.

Four: retreat to the web. Sell bookings on Sumiran's own site, where Exhibit 2's payer rate is 70 per cent. That number is real; the inference is not.

Five: play for time. Appeal, seek an interpretation, raise the question through an industry body, wait for the fee revisions expected on 1 January 2027. But the deadline is 30 October and the peak 8 November, so misjudging policy costs a pulled listing in the fortnight that cannot be repeated.

All five framings assume the disputed thirty per cent is the problem worth solving. Exhibit 1 says the stores take ₹236.40 lakh a month and suppliers ₹579.00 lakh, and the contracts governing the larger number expire in five months, on no agenda. Exhibit 5 says a fifth of the discovery Sumiran is protecting may be demand it bought itself; Exhibit 6 says the devotees who pay most arrive by name, not by browsing. It is not obvious that the app is the thing worth defending — and it is the one thing everybody has assumed.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The remediation deadline is Friday, 30 October. Diwali is 8 November and the peak runs through Kartik Purnima; last year the four weeks from Dhanteras carried a quarter of annual temple-service volume. The board meets on 2 November to release the Series B's second tranche, ₹85 crore of a ₹210 crore round led by Virasat Growth Capital, ₹125 crore of which was drawn in April. Two conditions attach: net retained revenue of at least 36 per cent of gross billings in the month before review, and no unremediated policy notice outstanding. Sumiran holds ₹38 crore of cash against ₹1.31 crore of monthly burn, so the tranche is a valuation question, not a survival one.

The supply agreements run to 31 March 2027 and bar any separate platform fee charged to the devotee. Engineering capacity is eleven engineer-days without touching the Diwali release, which freezes on 24 October. Counsel's view is that whatever Sumiran does must be explicable to an Indian regulator and to the store as the same decision, in the same words. Nobody has costed a second reclassification.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What is Sumiran buying with the ₹236.40 lakh a month it pays the stores, and which exhibit comes closest to measuring it?
  2. Exhibits 2 and 5 describe the same month and support opposite conclusions about store-driven discovery. What would you have to believe for each, and what test could separate them before 30 October?
  3. The February 2024 classification was defensible when made. Was it a mistake? Distinguish it from the failure to seek a ruling on it.
  4. Suppliers take ₹579.00 lakh a month against the stores' ₹236.40 lakh, under contracts expiring on 31 March 2027. Why is that absent from every option Sarayu has framed?
  5. Jatin Vora's line earns most per order, depends most on store billing and cannot use the consignment fix. Should the overseas and Indian products now diverge in classification, price and rail?
  6. It is Monday, 19 October. What does Sarayu instruct, in what order, with eleven engineer-days and no ruling from the store? Draft what she tells the board on 2 November if the app is compliant and the covenant missed — and what she tells it if the margin holds because she restructured the SKU in a way the store may later call avoidance.

11. Tonight

At a quarter to midnight Sarayu drafted an email asking for the classification in writing whichever way it went, and did not send it. Sending it invited the answer she did not want on the record eighteen days before the board met. Not sending it left her, for the second time in thirty-one months, deciding what the rule was rather than asking. She thought about the ninety minutes her mother used to drive, and how little of seven years' building was in the app, and how much in the store.

App Stores as a Channel

An app store is not one channel but three instruments bolted together: a discovery algorithm, a regulator and a tollbooth. Command begins with knowing which is aimed at your product.

1. Two decisions, one week apart

On 14 October 2026 Purva Deshpande sat in the Pattang Game Studios office in Aurangabad with one sheet from her finance lead, Zubin Datar. Pattang made casual games monetised entirely on in-app purchase; its live title, Gilli Rush, had 16,00,000 monthly iOS players. The sheet said 2026 App Store receipts would land at ₹10.40 crore gross, commission at ₹1.62 crore, and proceeds of ₹8.78 crore would put Pattang ₹28 lakh over the one-million-dollar line governing Apple’s Small Business Program — an overshoot costing ₹1.50 crore in 2027.

Eleven kilometres away, on 21 October, Pranali Gokhale faced the other face of the same channel. Zimmedari Service Cloud sold a field-service application — work orders, parts, proof of service, routing — to forty enterprise customers in lift and genset servicing. Twelve thousand technicians carried it at ₹450 a seat a month, ₹6.48 crore of annual recurring revenue. Zimmedari paid the stores almost nothing, since enterprise seats are contracted outside the app. What it paid was dependency: 8,400 of the 12,000 seats reached the app only by a technician installing it from the public store. Play’s background-location declaration was due on 30 October, and review could take two days or three weeks; nine customers, 2,700 seats and ₹1.458 crore of revenue held contracts promising continuous tracking.

Purva’s exposure was to the tollbooth and the algorithm; Pranali’s was to the regulator. Neither could have used the other’s playbook.

2. The idea, and the schools that disagree

An app store as a channel is one intermediary performing three separable functions. Discovery: the store ranks listings, and shaping a listing to that ranking is App Store Optimisation, or ASO — title, keyword field, screenshots, rating average, install conversion. Regulation: every binary and its metadata pass review against some 190 clauses, and the store may reject, delay or remove at discretion. Taxation: digital goods consumed in the app must route through the store’s payment rail, at a commission historically 30 per cent and now tiered toward 15.

The bundling answered a 2008 problem: distribution ran through carrier decks and per-handset porting, with carrier billing often above 40 per cent, so one storefront, one 70/30 split and global reach on day one sharply reduced transaction cost. The split held twelve years and broke under litigation rather than competition: Epic’s suits, the Competition Commission of India’s 2022 orders on Google’s billing mandate, the EU’s Digital Markets Act, the 2025 anti-steering injunction.

The channel-cost school signs: commission is acquisition cost, to be compared with the next-best channel. A ₹60 paid install returning ₹240 of lifetime gross pays a ₹72 toll — one more install’s worth of spend, for free demand. It will not call that a tax, because a tax buys nothing. The rent-extraction school signs the inverse: hosting a binary and clearing a card costs under five per cent of transaction value; the rest is rent secured by control of the handset. It will not sign that store discovery is worth 30 per cent to a product bought by a procurement committee. The dependency school signs neither figure: commission is the visible price; the invisible price is that a third party can change your product, pricing and availability without consent.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Begin with the tollbooth, where the arithmetic is least understood. At least four rules land on the number 15, sharing no mechanism. Apple’s Small Business Program charges 15 per cent to a developer whose App Store proceeds — receipts net of commission — were a million dollars or less in the previous calendar year; enrolment is by annual application. Separately, regardless of size, Apple charges 15 per cent once a particular subscriber has paid more than twelve continuous months. Google Play charges 15 per cent on the first million dollars of earnings in each year, automatically. And User Choice Billing, introduced in India after the CCI’s orders, trades points off the rate for the developer’s own processing.

Two of those decide Purva’s case: Apple tests the prior year’s proceeds, Google the current year’s earnings. At an indicative ₹85 to the dollar, a million dollars of proceeds is ₹8.50 crore. Because proceeds are 85 per cent of gross on the 15 per cent tier, the threshold in gross receipts is ₹8.50 crore divided by 0.85 — exactly ₹10.00 crore.

Three second-order effects follow, none visible in the blended rate. First, 15.58 per cent is a useless summary: the rate on the year’s last ₹40 lakh was 30 per cent. Second, the cliff: exceeding the prior-year test at all removes the tier for all of 2027. On a 2027 plan of ₹15.00 crore of store gross, eligibility means 15 per cent on the first ₹10.00 crore and 30 on the remaining ₹5.00 crore, ₹3.00 crore in all, a blended 20.00 per cent; ineligibility means a flat 30 per cent, ₹4.50 crore. The difference is ₹1.50 crore. Third, charge that penalty to the receipts that caused it and the last ₹40 lakh of 2026 carries ₹12 lakh of its own commission plus ₹1.50 crore of next year’s — a marginal rate of 405 per cent, illuminating as an incentive, indefensible in a board pack.

Now discovery. Pattang ran a Play listing experiment in November 2026: the same 2,31,000 product-page views to each arm, the variant changing only its screenshots.

Install rate is itself a ranking input, so a better-converting listing is shown more often and the measured 10 per cent understates the effect. The same compounding runs through ratings. Gilli Rush held 4.1 across 82,000 ratings, a rating sum of 3,36,200. Reaching 4.4 with x five-star ratings requires (3,36,200 + 5x) ÷ (82,000 + x) = 4.4, so 0.6x = 24,600 and x = 41,000 — forty-one thousand perfect ratings for three-tenths of a point.

4. When it applies, and when it misleads

The store is your discovery channel only if buyers search for products like yours. True for Pattang, where 84 per cent of installs begin in store search and browse; false for Zimmedari, whose buyer is a procurement committee. Nobody browses Play for lift-maintenance software.

Commission applies only where digital goods are consumed inside the app. True of all Pattang revenue; true of only the ₹9.00 lakh a month Zimmedari sells self-serve, 14.29 per cent of its ₹7.56 crore of annualised revenue. The rest is contracted and exempt.

Policy exposure scales with the share of delivery that depends on a public listing, not the share of revenue that pays commission. Here the standard framing becomes actively misleading: Zimmedari pays almost no toll and is the more store-dependent company, because a removal stops 8,400 technicians working the same afternoon.

The tiers are worth designing around only near a threshold. Purva is ₹28 lakh from one, so for her it dominates the quarter; a company at ₹80 crore of store gross should stop thinking about tiers altogether.

5. Hard edge cases, and the organisational seams

Apple assesses its threshold at the developer account, not the app, so a second title’s success pushes the first onto the higher rate — hence the arguments about separate legal entities. Two-sided products hit a sharper line: a marketplace intermediating a real-world service owes no commission, while the same app selling a digital badge does, so the commissionable boundary runs through the product itself. Regulated categories carry two rulebooks: a lending app must satisfy the Reserve Bank’s digital-lending directions and Play’s personal-loan policy, whose demands are stricter and whose reviewers are not lawyers. For hardware the toll barely applies and the regulator absolutely does, the companion app being the only way to commission a device. AI-native products face the newest edge: inference at ₹9 a session cannot absorb 30 per cent on a ₹399 subscription.

The seam is where failures happen. Zimmedari’s location declaration is nominally product, but continuous tracking sits in nine signed contracts, the permission is an engineering choice, and the disclosure text the reviewer reads is written by whoever is free. Mature companies make one person accountable across all three functions and keep an interpretation log of every ruling received. What they say they keep is a checklist; what they do is remember.

6. Eight distinctions that separate an expert

The blended rate is a reporting number, not a decision number. Pattang’s 15.58 per cent is correct and empty: no decision Purva makes is priced there. The tell is a team that quotes its take rate to two decimals but cannot say what the next rupee costs.

Apple’s threshold is on proceeds; Google’s on current-year earnings. The same ₹10.40 crore of gross costs ₹1.62 crore on the App Store and ₹1.845 crore on Play — a blended 17.74 per cent against 15.58 — and only Apple’s has a next-year cliff. The tell is a forecast applying one store’s tier logic to both.

Off-store revenue does not count toward the threshold. That, not rate arbitrage, is the reason to build a web shop early. The tell is a team justifying direct checkout purely on the 30 per cent, and so building it a year late.

Review is precedent-driven, not rule-driven. The same feature is approved for one app and refused for another, because reviewers apply clauses through judgement informed by prior cases, including prior cases on your account. The tell is a team reading the guidelines like a compiler specification.

A permission review is a different animal from a build review. Zimmedari’s binaries clear in two days; its sensitive-permission declarations have taken eighteen. The tell is a calendar with one two-day store block whatever the release contains.

Rating averages are stocks, not flows. Forty-one thousand five-star ratings to move 4.1 to 4.4 is a denominator that never resets; the obvious reading, that a good release fixes a rating, is wrong at any scale. The same loop runs through install rate: a listing winning installs from players who quit on day one is demoted by the algorithm that promoted it.

The enterprise carve-out is narrower than sales teams believe. Zimmedari is exempt because the organisation buys and provisions seats; the moment a technician can upgrade their own account in the app, the transaction is commissionable, enforced against the product as shipped, not the contract as signed. The tell is a self-serve upgrade button added for convenience.

Platform risk is measured in delivery, not revenue. What matters is the share of users who cannot receive your software if the listing disappears: 70 per cent for Zimmedari, 100 for Pattang.

7. Product type and company stage

For consumer products all three instruments apply and discovery dominates; commission is a cost of goods sold, not a strategy question. For B2B and enterprise the store is a distribution utility and a regulator, so the posture is minimising exposure: managed private distribution wherever customer IT allows, a deliberately boring public listing, no commissionable surfaces in the enterprise build. Marketplaces carry the boundary inside the product and must staff for it; hardware should treat review as a manufacturing dependency. AI products are unresolved, marginal cost being high enough that 30 per cent can invert gross margin.

By stage the differences are fewer than claimed. A pre-revenue company should ignore tiers and optimise its listing, its constraint being installs. A company near the threshold should treat it as a planning variable while it is near it. What does not change is the regulator: a twelve-person studio and a listed company face the same reviewer and rulebook.

8. Three worked examples

Pattang’s web shop: a rate argument that was really a threshold argument

Purva’s biggest spenders are concentrated enough to make a direct channel feasible. In a representative month of the Q4 2026 plan, with every rupee on the store:

The comparison must be made per rupee of list price, including what a web shop introduces: the switching discount, gateway fees, fraud, failed-payment support.

That is incomplete, because a web checkout converts worse than a one-tap purchase. Let k be the fraction of redirected demand that completes on the web. Migration pays when 85.81k exceeds the store’s net: break-even k is 85.00 ÷ 85.81 = 99.06 per cent against the 15 per cent tier and 70.00 ÷ 85.81 = 81.58 per cent against 30. Pattang’s pilot measured 88 per cent.

So on the 15 per cent tier the shop is worth almost nothing on rate alone. Redirecting ₹30.00 lakh of the high-spend segment’s ₹66.00 lakh leaves ₹26.40 lakh completing on the web and ₹3.60 lakh returning to in-app purchase, so the segment’s store receipts become ₹39.60 lakh. The ₹26.40 lakh yields ₹22.65 lakh net against ₹22.44 lakh on the store at 15 per cent: a gain of ₹21,384 a month. Against a 30 per cent tier it gains ₹4.17 lakh. The build costs ₹14.67 lakh fully loaded — a payback of 68.6 months at 15 per cent and 3.5 months at 30.

The decisive number lies elsewhere: web receipts are not App Store receipts and do not count toward the threshold. Running the shop from 1 October cuts Q4 store gross by ₹26.40 lakh a month to ₹2.808 crore, and 2026 store gross to ₹9.608 crore — below the ₹10.00 crore crossing point, so the year stays at 15 per cent. Commission falls to ₹1.4412 crore and proceeds to ₹8.1668 crore, or $960,800: ₹33.32 lakh under the line, preserving ₹1.50 crore of 2027 value. In-year net receipts, with the shop’s ₹67.96 lakh, come to ₹8.8464 crore against ₹8.78 crore.

Zimmedari’s self-serve tier: a blended rate computed, not assumed

Zimmedari’s 1,500 self-serve seats bill ₹600 a month through in-app purchase, ₹9,00,000 of gross, booked by finance at 30 per cent, ₹2,70,000. In fact 825 seats had passed twelve continuous months and dropped to 15 per cent: ₹4,95,000 at 15 per cent is ₹74,250, and the remaining 675 first-year seats, ₹4,05,000 at 30 per cent, cost ₹1,21,500. Commission of ₹1,95,750 on ₹9,00,000 is a blended 21.75 per cent, and net receipts ₹7,04,250 against the planned ₹6,30,000.

Panghat Interactive: the failure, and what recovery cost

Panghat Interactive, a casual studio in Indore, had from 1 October 2025 routed every coin purchase through a webview to its own checkout, paying a 2.4 per cent gateway fee and no commission. On iOS gross of ₹92.00 lakh a month that was worth ₹25.39 lakh a month against compliant purchase at 30 per cent — ₹114.26 lakh over four and a half months. On 12 February 2026 Apple removed the app; it returned on 3 March with a reset ranking.

Two costs never reached that table. A ₹3.20 crore co-marketing commitment from Zohal Interactive FZ-LLC, a Dubai publisher, lapsed when availability could not be guaranteed; and Apple placed the account under heightened review for ninety days. Recovery was unglamorous: compliant purchase, the Small Business Program, seven months rebuilding rank, and only then a web shop built the permitted way — no link inside the app — carrying 31 per cent of high-spend receipts within a year.

9. Failure modes and early warnings

Planning a launch against the median review time. Sign: a two-day store block on the calendar whatever the release contains. Diagnostic: what is the ninetieth percentile of our own review times, by submission type?

A commissionable surface inside an exempt product. Sign: a self-serve upgrade path in an enterprise build. Diagnostic: can a user increase what we bill them, without their employer, from inside the app? At review it costs a release; in an audit, retroactive commission.

Mistaking no commission for no dependency. Sign: no answer to what happens if the listing goes down tomorrow. Diagnostic: what share of users cannot receive our software without the public store?

Building the off-store channel with an in-app link. Sign: a growth experiment whose mechanism is a button that leaves the app. Diagnostic: would this survive a reviewer reading the anti-steering clause against us? That was Panghat’s mistake, at ₹1.26 crore and a publisher.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Commission is fair payment for a channel, and attacking it is a distraction. The evidence: global payment, tax handling, fraud liability, refunds, free demand. On the 15 per cent tier Pattang’s own web shop returned ₹21,384 a month for four engineer-months. For this to be wrong, direct channels would have to convert nearly as well as in-app purchase, which at 88 per cent completion among the most motivated segment they do not.

The toll is rent, and any product that can build a direct relationship should. The evidence is the gap at the higher tier — ₹15.81 per ₹100 of list price, a 3.5-month payback — and that the store contributed nothing to Zimmedari’s discovery yet charged 21.75 per cent on its self-serve seats. For this to be wrong, hidden off-store costs would have to close the gap, which practitioners here concede are underestimated by half.

Only delivery dependency matters; the other two argue about margin while standing on someone else’s floor. Its evidence is every removal case, Panghat’s included, where commission saved was dwarfed by availability lost. For this to be wrong, removals would have to be rare and quickly reversible for compliant products — which, for compliant products, they largely are.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this recites the tiers. Someone who has internalised it asks what the next rupee costs rather than the average, and so sees cliffs early; separates the three instruments before diagnosing; treats the store as a counterparty with a memory; and plans against the distribution of review outcomes, not its median.

12. What each of them decided

Purva approved the web shop on 29 October 2026, for the threshold rather than the rate. The ₹21,384 a month it earns on the current tier does not justify four engineer-months, but holding 2026 proceeds at ₹8.1668 crore rather than ₹8.78 crore preserves ₹1.50 crore of 2027 commission, and the shop will be worth ₹4.17 lakh a month the year Pattang crosses for real.

Pranali chose differently. She filed the declaration on 27 October, its disclosure text written by her counsel rather than an engineer, and shipped a geofenced check-in fallback behind a feature flag, so a refusal would degrade the product for nine customers rather than block the release for forty. She also began the work that addresses her real risk: moving customers onto managed private distribution, targeting 70 per cent of seats by March 2028. Her note to the board carried one line: we do not pay the store much, which is precisely why nobody here was watching it.

Discussion questions. (1) Purva justified four engineer-months on a ₹1.50 crore threshold effect rather than a ₹21,384 monthly margin. Is next year’s tier eligibility a sound basis for that? (2) Zimmedari pays commission on 14.29 per cent of revenue and depends on the store for 70 per cent of delivery. Which number should govern its strategy, and who owns it? (3) What evidence would have changed your answer on Panghat’s checkout in September 2025?

13. Going deeper

  • Channels: paid, owned, earned — the store beside its competitors for the same budget.
  • Mobile platform constraints — why Pranali’s problem was a declaration.
  • Consumer acquisition channels — what an ASO lift is valued against.
  • Consumer subscriptions and in-app purchase — the twelve-month rule, modelled.
  • Platform dependency risk — pricing a dependency you cannot remove.
  • What a GTM strategy is — all channels chosen together.
  • Your first 100 users — why early teams ignore the tiers.
  • Inbound vs outbound — an engine for Pattang, an irrelevance for Zimmedari.
  • Product-led growth — the canonical product-led channel.
  • Sales-led growth — the model behind Zimmedari’s exempt revenue.
  • Product-led sales (PQA / PQL) — store-acquired accounts becoming exempt contracts.

App Stores as a Channel

ASO, review, policy, and the 15–30% question: how the App Store and Play Store shape what a mobile product can charge, promise, and ship.

1. A number that would not add up

On the morning of 8 September 2026, Saloni Doshi, VP of Growth and Platform at Sargam Streams, sat in the company's office off Kaloor Junction in Kochi and read a submission notice from Apple's App Review team. Sargam Streams ran a regional-language audio app — Malayalam, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Hindi music, devotional albums and independent artist catalogues — sold on a ₹150-a-month subscription called Sangeet Plus, plus one-off purchases: album unlocks, concert recordings, and a new artist "tip jar" feature built for Navratri. The notice flagged the tip jar under Guideline 3.1.1, the rule that any purchase of digital content consumed inside the app must go through Apple's own payment system. Saloni's team had wired the tip jar to a lighter payment sheet already built for the web version. It worked. It was also, on Apple's reading, exactly the workaround the guideline existed to stop.

The timing mattered more than the fix. Sargam Streams' Diwali push — a revamped store listing, new screenshots in four languages, and the tip jar as its centrepiece — was booked to go live on 20 October, the start of the festival's gifting season. App Review's stated turnaround was one to two days, but a rejected build meant a second queue with no guarantee of clearing before media spend began. Company-wide, Sargam Streams' iOS in-app receipts already ran at ₹4.80 crore a month, of which Apple's standard 30% commission took ₹1.44 crore, leaving ₹3.36 crore net. A blocked release meant the campaign built to grow that base would open the season with a marquee feature switched off. Saloni had six days to decide what to fix, what to defend, and what to leave for later.

2. The idea

An app store is not a shelf. It is a channel with its own rules of entry, its own tollbooth, and its own editor between the product and the customer. Concretely: an app store as a channel means Apple's App Store and Google's Play Store function as (a) the primary discovery surface, governed by App Store Optimisation or ASO — shaping a listing's title, keywords, screenshots and ratings so search and browse algorithms surface it; (b) a gatekeeper, through app review, that can approve, reject or remove a build against published policy; and (c) a payment processor taking a commission, historically 30% and now tiered toward 15% under specific conditions.

The idea took shape gradually. Apple opened the App Store in July 2008 with a flat 70/30 split and a human review queue; Google's Play Store followed the same 30% a year later, with lighter review. The split stayed unchanged for a decade until regulatory pressure — Epic Games' lawsuits, the EU's Digital Markets Act, and in India the CCI's 2022 order against Google's billing mandate — forced both companies to carve out lower tiers and alternative billing paths. The sentence Saloni could say in a meeting without sounding glib: "the store is not a distribution partner, it is a second regulator, and its commission is the price of a customer relationship we don't fully own."

3. How it actually works

Three mechanisms run in parallel, and a mobile product manager has to operate all three at once. The first is discovery. A store listing has a small set of levers — title, subtitle, a hidden keyword field (100 characters on iOS), screenshots, a preview video, category, and the weight of ratings and review velocity. The store's search and browse algorithms rank listings against these signals and against how many viewers actually install, so ASO is two disciplines wearing one name: getting found and converting once found.

The second mechanism is review. Every build passes through an automated and human check against a published guideline document — roughly 190 clauses under safety, performance, business, design and legal headings. New teams treat this as a formality; the implicit step is that review covers the metadata around a build, not only its code — an overpromising screenshot can trigger rejection on its own. Sargam Streams' own history makes the point: of 14 iOS releases in the past year, 9 cleared first-pass and 5 did not.

The third mechanism is the commission, and this is where the "15–30% question" actually lives, because at least three different 15% rates get conflated into one. Apple's Small Business Program drops the commission to 15% for any developer whose total App Store revenue was under one million US dollars in the prior calendar year — roughly ₹8.3 crore at an indicative ₹83-to-the-dollar rate — applied for annually. Separately, regardless of size, Apple drops the commission on an individual subscriber's auto-renewing subscription from 30% to 15% once that subscriber has been continuously subscribed past twelve months, a loyalty discount rather than a small-business one. Google's Play Store runs a third structure: 15% automatically on a developer's first million dollars of annual revenue, 30% above it, no application needed. A team that has only heard "apps pay 15 to 30%" and never separated these three will misprice a forecast the first time it matters.

4. A worked example: what a store-listing rebuild is actually worth

Separately from the tip-jar problem, Saloni's team had spent six weeks rebuilding the iOS store listing for Diwali: new keywords, localised screenshots, a refreshed preview video. Before approving spend on paid installs behind it, she asked her analyst to show the arithmetic line by line, using the campaign's projected 10,00,000 store page views as the shared starting point for both listings.

The install rate is the only assumption that moves between the two columns; every later row follows from it mechanically, at fixed 25% trial-start and 35% paid-conversion rates. At the standard 30% first-year commission, the net difference works out to ₹31,23,750 minus ₹25,72,500 — ₹5,51,250 of extra net receipts every month, from a rebuild costing roughly three weeks of one designer's time. That number justified the ASO spend on its own, independent of the tip jar.

A second pass, run once retention data from an earlier cohort arrived, showed the other side of the 15–30% question. Of the 24,500 baseline subscribers, roughly 40% would still be subscribed past their twelfth month — 9,800 subscribers — and Apple's subscription-longevity rule drops the commission on exactly that group from 30% to 15%, no application required. Those 9,800 second-year subscribers generate ₹14,70,000 of monthly gross, taxed at 15% for ₹2,20,500, leaving ₹12,49,500 net — a materially better margin than the first-year cohort ever carried, purely from time passing.

5. The nuances a learner has to sit with

ASO earns attention; it cannot fix the product.

A better keyword field and screenshot set moved the install rate from 28% to 34% because the product already retained the users who arrived. ASO changes who walks through the door, not what they find inside; teams chasing install-rate gains while ignoring retention optimise the number a store rewards least.

Review guidelines are precedent-based, not code-based.

The same feature can be approved for one app and rejected for another, because App Review applies its clauses through human judgement informed by prior cases. Treating the guideline document as a compiler to satisfy exactly is a common source of surprise rejections.

The three 15% rates are not one rate.

Apple's Small Business Program, Apple's subscription-longevity discount, and Google's automatic first-million tier all land at 15%, by coincidence rather than a shared mechanism. A forecast that says "we're on the 15% tier," without saying which, is not yet a forecast.

Store commission applies to in-app transactions, not to the business.

Sargam Streams could sell Sangeet Plus on its own website at full price, commission-free; the 15–30% question only arises for purchases initiated inside the app. Teams often overstate the store's reach into revenue that never touches its payment sheet.

A rejection is a negotiation, not a verdict.

Apple's App Review Board hears appeals, and a specific, evidence-backed appeal — citing a comparable approved app, or clarifying a misread feature — succeeds often enough that treating the first rejection as final wastes a window a launch rarely affords.

India's regulatory posture is already reshaping the toll.

Following the CCI's 2022 order, Google now runs a User Choice Billing programme in India letting a developer route payments through its own processor at roughly a four-point discount off the standard commission, bearing the processor's fee separately — real relief, but cost shifted, not removed.

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and small versus large

Consumer subscription apps like Sargam Streams live and die by ASO, since most users arrive from search or browse with no prior brand relationship, and commission bites on a high volume of small, recurring transactions. B2B software mostly sidesteps the store: enterprise buyers are sold to directly through a website contract. Marketplaces face the sharpest version of the policy question, since Apple and Google exempt a marketplace connecting buyers to real-world services (a ride, a delivery) from in-app commission while treating digital goods differently — a line Sargam Streams had to draw between its subscriptions (commissionable) and its live-event ticket referrals to venues (not). Scale matters too: a small studio under the threshold benefits from Apple's Small Business Program, while a company Sargam Streams' size wins its margin through subscriber longevity and its own web checkout instead.

7. Common mistakes

Treating the store listing as marketing collateral, finished once. Symptom: a screenshot set untouched for two years while install rates decay. The error is believing ASO is a launch task, not a maintained surface. Cheap diagnostic: check the listing's last-edit date against recently updated top competitors.

Submitting a policy-sensitive feature without a fallback. Symptom: a launch date that slips a full review cycle after a first rejection. The error is designing one version and assuming approval, rather than a compliant fallback in parallel. Cheap diagnostic: ask, before submission, what the feature looks like if the relevant guideline is read against you.

Quoting one blended commission number to the board. Symptom: a forecast wrong by several margin points within two quarters. The error is averaging first- and second-year subscription commission, or Apple and Google rates, into one "store take." Cheap diagnostic: ask which of the three 15% rates the number assumes.

8. What good looks like

At a comparable regional-audio competitor, product and legal reviewed every new in-app payment surface against the guideline document before a line of code was written, and kept a documented fallback for anything touching Guideline 3.1.1. Their Diwali-season release drew one review question, resolved by email in four hours, no rejection, no slipped date — a predictable regulator rather than a surprise one, because the guideline reading was already done.

9. What Saloni decided

Saloni split the two problems apart. She pulled the tip jar's payment sheet back onto Apple's own in-app purchase system for the iOS build only, accepting the 30% commission on that feature rather than risking the entire submission, and kept the cheaper web-native sheet for Android and the website, where Guideline 3.1.1 does not apply. The store-listing rebuild shipped unchanged. The resubmission cleared review in a day and a half, comfortably inside the campaign's runway. Sanaya Parekh, the company's counsel, logged the interpretation in a shared policy document so the next review would not relitigate it. Next on Saloni's list: Google Play's User Choice Billing option, and acquisition channels more broadly, because the store had just shown her that discovery, policy and pricing are one decision wearing three names. Two questions worth sitting with: whose job is it to read the guidelines before a feature is built, rather than after? And if commission rates diverge this much by tenure and geography, is "our take rate" even a single number a forecast should trust?

Parvah Wellness and the App-Store Clock

Bengaluru, Monday, 28 September 2026

1. The morning the review flag arrived

Priyanka Prabhu, founder and chief executive of Parvah Wellness Private Limited, was at her desk in the company's Indiranagar office reading an email from Apple's India developer-relations team. The subject line read: App Review Guideline 3.1.1 — action required within 10 days. Build 6.3 of the Parvah Plus app, approved three weeks earlier, showed a banner to iOS users after their third session inviting them to "manage your subscription at parvahwellness.in." Apple's reviewers had reclassified this as an anti-steering violation. Priyanka had ten days, until Thursday, 8 October, to fix it or the app would be pulled from the India App Store.

The timing was poor. Parvah's Navratri campaign was set to go live on 21 October, the highest-converting fortnight of the wellness calendar. Six days after Apple's deadline, on 14 October, Priyanka faced a call with the lead investor in Parvah's Series B, whose diligence team had flagged app-store commissions as the largest drag on gross margin. She now had ten days to decide how to comply, and what to do about a second, unrelated matter sitting half-built in her backlog: Google Play's User Choice Billing, newly available to more subscription categories in India since July.

2. Parvah Wellness

Priyanka started Parvah Wellness in 2019 after five years running studio operations for a Bengaluru fitness chain, convinced Indians wanting structured movement, sleep, and meditation guidance would rather follow it from a phone than pay for a studio membership. Parvah Plus, the paid tier, bundles guided fitness routines, sleep soundscapes, and meditation audio in English and six Indian languages; a free tier carries ads and a limited library. The company competes with Cult.fit and HealthifyMe among India's home-grown fitness apps, and with Calm and Headspace among premium, English-first subscribers in the metros and the Gulf diaspora.

Distribution runs almost entirely through the two app stores: search inside the Apple App Store and Google Play accounts for 59,500 of Parvah's roughly 85,000 monthly new installs, 70 per cent, with the rest split across referral and paid social. Of Parvah's 6,00,000 monthly active users, 48,000, 8 per cent, pay for Parvah Plus. A direct-billing option on Parvah's own website has existed since 2023 but carries only 7,200 of those 48,000, 15 per cent, since nearly all discovery, trust, and checkout still happens inside the stores. Parvah raised its Series A in 2022 and now has a signed Series B term sheet expected to close in Q4 2026, subject to diligence that includes gross margin.

3. What each side of the business sees

Two things are true on 28 September, and Priyanka's team does not agree on how they connect. Apple's letter is unambiguous: fix the banner or lose the India listing before Navratri. Google's User Choice Billing, which lets an Android user pick Parvah's own payment processor at checkout instead of Google's, has sat half-built since August, when Gautam Nagpal's Pune team prototyped the picker screen and paused, waiting to see how the Apple matter resolved before spending more sprint time on it.

From Pune, Gautam estimates the Android build is nine to ten engineer-days, deliverable before 8 October if he reassigns two engineers now. From Toronto, data scientist Nandita Ghosh runs the numbers the other way: her churn model estimates that if the app disappears from India search for even a short window in the festive weeks, roughly 8 per cent of the 40,800 subscribers billed through the two stores would fail to renew or reinstall in time, since so much of Parvah's renewal traffic depends on being findable in store search, not any channel it owns. From New Jersey, Girish Nanda, who owns the investor relationship, wants a credible margin improvement to point to ahead of 14 October, without adding fresh risk to a round close to closing.

4. The people

Priyanka Prabhu — Founder & CEO, Bengaluru (HQ). Wants the app live through Navratri, a clean margin story, and a decision she will not need to reverse under pressure.

Gautam Nagpal — Head of Engineering, Pune. Wants a plan he can staff and finish once, not rebuild because a decision came late.

Nandita Ghosh — Lead Data Scientist, Toronto. Wants the decision grounded in her churn numbers, not a gut call that ignores the visibility risk.

Girish Nanda — Head of Revenue & Partnerships, New Jersey. Wants a defensible margin narrative for 14 October that does not read as reckless two weeks from closing.

6. An illustration: the ten-day window

7. The options

Option A — Comply on iOS, hold Android as is

Remove the banner before 8 October, keep both stores on existing terms, and postpone Android User Choice Billing until after the Series B closes. Lowest risk: it protects the India listing and Navratri outright. Cost: ₹25.92 lakh a year of sanctioned margin left unclaimed, and nothing new for Girish to tell the board beyond "we are compliant."

Option B — Comply on iOS, and switch on Android User Choice Billing now

Remove the banner, and in parallel have Gautam's team finish the Android picker already prototyped, moving the 21,600 Google Play subscribers onto User Choice Billing before 8 October. This lifts net by ₹2.16 lakh a month, ₹25.92 lakh a year, on a mechanism Google has sanctioned for India, in a build Gautam can finish with engineers already familiar with the prototype. Cost: a second checkout design for support to learn, and a short scramble alongside the compliance fix.

Option C — Use the window to push steering harder on both stores

Rather than remove the banner, extend a similar "manage elsewhere" prompt to Android too, betting enforcement will be inconsistent. If it worked on both platforms with no penalty, the ceiling is ₹3.18 crore a year in avoided commission. But Apple has already flagged this exact behaviour once, in writing, with a deadline; doing more of it invites the removal it threatens, at the one moment — ten days before Navratri — when Nandita's model says removal is costliest, since store search drives 70 per cent of installs and most renewals.

8. Questions for discussion

  1. What is Parvah buying with the ₹31.32 lakh a month it pays in commission and gateway fees (Exhibit 1), and does that change by channel?
  2. How should Priyanka weigh Girish's need for a certain, near-term margin number against Nandita's uncertain but plausible cost to ASO-driven growth?
  3. Is switching on Android User Choice Billing while removing the same prompt from iOS a consistent position, or does it just move the tension?
  4. Given what is achievable by 8 October, what should Girish tell the board on 14 October about Parvah's margin trajectory?

A note for the learner

App stores are a distribution channel, a billing system, and a policy regime at once; the three cannot be optimised one at a time. Parvah's 15–30 per cent commission is not simply a tax on revenue earned elsewhere: it is priced into a bundle that also delivers the search visibility behind 70 per cent of new installs and most renewals. Treating the commission line as separable from the review-policy risk and the ASO dependency — as Option C does — can look like the best move on a spreadsheet while being the most dangerous one in practice, because it risks the channel's discovery value to save money on its billing cut.

The defensible path is Option B. Complying by 8 October is not optional, since losing the India listing before Navratri would cost far more than any commission saved elsewhere — by Nandita's estimate, ₹16.32 lakh a month against Parvah's store-billed base. Switching on Android User Choice Billing at the same time is the one lever that is both Google-sanctioned in India and already engineered: it adds ₹25.92 lakh a year of durable margin without touching the iOS question or the ASO channel Parvah depends on. Option C's larger number is real only if enforcement does not happen, which is exactly what Apple's letter has just ruled out. A well-reasoned answer takes the certain fix first, takes the sanctioned gain ready to ship, and leaves full steering on both platforms for after the Series B closes and India policy shifts, not before.

Launch Tiers and Launch Readiness

Sizing the launch to the release — and what to do when reach, readiness and reversibility disagree.

1. Two mornings in Tirupati

On 8 June 2026, eleven days before the first sowing rains were forecast over Rayalaseema, Sailaja Gollapudi sat down with a release slate she could not ship as written. Gollapudi was chief product officer of Yashaswi Krishi Networks, a Tirupati platform selling seed, crop-protection and nutrition inputs to cotton, chilli and pulses growers through 1,860 dealer outlets, bundled with agronomy advisory, soil testing and a dealer-credit ledger. Last year 1,15,000 growers transacted at an average ₹24,000: gross merchandise value ₹276 crore, gross profit at a blended 9.5 per cent ₹26.22 crore.

Five releases were finished. One — a spray-window advisory telling chilli growers when thrips pressure justified a particular mode-of-action rotation — would touch 46,000 of the 1,15,000 transacting growers (40 per cent) and put ₹519.8 lakh of crop-protection merchandise through a changed recommendation path in sixty days: the year's largest launch on any scoring Yashaswi had written down. Only a qualified agronomist could answer its questions, and Yashaswi's 64 agronomists were already at 85.4 per cent of escalation capacity.

Four kilometres away, Raghuram Kanchustambham, head of product at Baadal Agronomy Systems, had the opposite problem. Baadal sold a soil-moisture sensing stake at ₹4,800 with a ₹1,200 annual subscription: 21,400 nodes across 7,300 farms, each governing a block averaging 2.1 acres. Firmware 3.2 revised the irrigation-trigger threshold; no screen changed and no grower would see a release note. But 3,650 of the 21,400 nodes (17.1 per cent) sat on connectivity too intermittent for a guaranteed rollback inside a crop cycle, and a trigger four points too dry at chilli flowering costs about 4 per cent of yield: ₹7,200 an acre on ₹1,80,000 of gross value. Across the 7,665 acres governed by unreachable nodes, ₹5.52 crore of grower crop value — within half a per cent of Baadal's annual revenue of ₹5.54 crore, of which ₹2.57 crore is subscription on 21,400 nodes.

Gollapudi's release scored as a major launch and could not be supported at that size; Kanchustambham's scored as nothing and could end his company. The framework, applied literally, failed both.

2. The idea, and the argument it settles

A launch tier is a pre-agreed classification of the coordinated effort a release earns — announcement, enablement, documentation, staffing, rollback planning — set by its effect on the outside world, not by the effort that produced it. A readiness gate separately decides whether the organisation is fit to execute that tier. Most failures here come from collapsing the two.

It has two uneasy ancestors. Release engineering graded changes by blast radius, and the grade set how much review and rollback planning was mandatory. The marketing launch calendar used tiers to ration a finite stock of customer attention. One asks how much damage this can do, the other how much noise it deserves; answering both with one number is convenient and unstable.

Three schools resolve that instability differently, each on a proposition specific enough to sign.

The scoring school holds that tiering must be a written, auditable function of reach and exposure, computed before any calendar exists. It will sign: a release's tier must be derivable by someone who did not build it. It will not sign that the score is sufficient. Its strength is removing the loudest voice in the room; its weakness, scoring what is easy to count.

The progressive-delivery school holds that tiers are an artefact of batch shipping and the real control is the exposure ramp: ship to 1 per cent, watch, ramp. It will sign: where the exposed fraction is yours to set, "how big is this launch?" becomes "how fast do we ramp?" It will not sign that announcement ramps the same way — a field-day campaign is single-shot, and a press mention cannot be undone at 3 per cent.

The readiness-first school, strongest in regulated and field-service businesses, holds the gate to be the decision and the tier its consequence. It will sign: no release may be announced beyond the audience the field organisation can serve in the worst plausible week. It will not sign that reach should be scored first, because scoring creates a commitment operations must argue against.

3. Mechanics: three axes, one gate, and a model that ranks options

Expert practice scores three axes, not two. Reach is the share of the active base whose workflow changes, not the share that could use the feature. Economic exposure is the merchandise, credit or refundable liability passing through the changed path in a defined window; the window matters, since a seasonal business concentrates a year into eight weeks. Reversibility, the speed and completeness of undoing, is the third axis — and the one most often folded into the others, where it disappears. Yashaswi's rule: Tier 1 needed reach of 25 per cent or more of the affected base, exposure of ₹500 lakh or more, or any change to a dose, label or statutory recommendation; Tier 2, reach of 5 to 25 per cent or exposure of ₹50 to ₹500 lakh. A rollback beyond 24 hours raised the tier a step; an irreversible change floored it at Tier 2.

4. The conditions, stated as testable claims

Claim 1. Tiering pays only when launch machinery is material against the release's economic effect. Gollapudi: ₹19.10 lakh of machinery against ₹28.46 lakh of gross profit. Kanchustambham: a ₹3.10 lakh staged ring against a ₹5.52 crore downside — true for the reverse reason.
Claim 2. Reach must be measurable before release. True at Yashaswi, where reach is a segment query; weak at Baadal, where fleet connectivity is known only probabilistically — why its tiers had been wrong for two years.
Claim 3. Announcement intensity drives adoption. True for the advisory, where dealer-led enablement moves adoption from 8 to 45 per cent. False for firmware, where adoption is total the moment it lands: the tier controls only whether anyone was warned.

The framework is actively misleading in three situations. Where exposure is involuntary — forced firmware, mandatory migration, statutory change — reach is always total and the tier degenerates into a communications choice: how Baadal scored its most dangerous release at Tier 3. Where the release is a withdrawal, the affected population is exactly those who used the thing, so reach must be measured on usage. And on a two-sided platform, one tier for both sides is an error.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

The hardware case is sharpest, because reversibility is physical. Baadal's over-the-air rollback reached 12,400 of the 21,400 nodes (57.9 per cent) within six hours, 17,750 (82.9 per cent) within forty-eight and 20,100 (93.9 per cent) within thirty days; 1,300 — 6.1 per cent — waited for a field engineer. A fleet has a rollback distribution, not a rollback time, and the tier belongs to the tail.

Figure 3 — Baadal's rollback distribution. The 6.1 per cent tail, roughly 2,730 acres, makes a silent firmware release a Tier 1 decision however few screens changed.

Two-sided products force two tiers from one release. The credit-limit engine was Tier 1 on the dealer side — 1,190 of the 1,860 outlets (64 per cent), ₹1,240 lakh of exposure — and Tier 3 on the grower side, where nothing changed unless a dealer's limit fell far enough to stop supply. The seam is organisational: dealer enablement sat with Anasuya Kottapalli's sales team in Guntur, grower communication with Jhansi Tallapaneni's advisory team, and the two disagreed on what Tier 1 obliged.

Regulated changes carry a floor scoring cannot lower: a revised dose sits under the Insecticides Act regime, a seed-lot record under the Seeds Act, a grade description under the Fertiliser Control Order. Yashaswi evaluated its veto before reach, because a compliance failure is not a support cost.

AI-native releases break tiering more subtly. When recommendations come from a model rather than a rule table, reach is a distribution over inputs, and behaviour changes on inputs nobody has seen. Yashaswi's thrips model was evaluated on 4,200 scouting records; nothing asked what happened on the 5 per cent of fields the training set barely represented. Mature companies run a shadow period — the new model beside the old, disagreements counted rather than acted on — then tier by disagreement rate, not user count. Few do so before sowing, when it costs a season.

6. Eight distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Tier measures effect on the outside world, not internal significance

Tier is not effort, and the subtler substitution is tier tracking political importance. The tell is a release whose tier rose after an executive asked about it: leadership attention signals internal salience, which tracks customer effect only loosely.

The gate can veto a tier; a clean gate cannot promote one

Readiness is necessary, not sufficient. The tell is a team that finishes its checklist early and argues the release now deserves a bigger launch — a search for return on sunk preparation cost, sound about effort, unsound about customers.

Silent is a decision about push, never about record

Tier 3 removes the campaign, never the changelog, help article or dealer note. The tell is a support agent learning of a change from a grower; the record is also the only defence when a state agriculture department asks, months later, what the platform advised.

Reach is measured on the workflow, not the feature

The competent practitioner counts users who can see the feature; the expert counts those whose behaviour changes, a larger set for any withdrawal or default change. The tell is a reach estimate that is a round fraction of the base — divided rather than queried.

Reversibility is an axis, not a footnote

The tell is a document with two axes and a closing sentence about rollback. Fold reversibility into exposure and you lose the distinction between a large reversible change and a small irreversible one — the two cases where tiering pays. Baadal's history is this mistake.

Seasonality changes the denominator, not only the date

A grower business has no twelve equal months. Gollapudi's headroom of 280 was a pre-sowing figure; in February the same agronomists had headroom above 900. The tell is a framework whose thresholds are annual; an expert states them against the release's own window.

Phasing is tier execution, not tier demotion

The tell is a status note reading "downgraded to Tier 2, phased" — two decisions collapsed into one. A phased Tier 1 keeps the enablement and rations exposure over time; Tier 2 forgoes it permanently. Where the dealer relationship is the channel, that compounds.

The model's job is elimination, not selection

The commonest expert error is over-trusting the ranking. Exhibit 2 separates phased Tier 1 from Tier 2 by ₹0.72 lakh, about 6.7 per cent of the smaller figure — inside the error on an adoption assumption nobody had measured. At 26 per cent adoption rather than 22, Tier 2 nets ₹13.25 lakh and wins. The model robustly kills only the silent and all-at-once options.

Where the difference is not real: the gate. Its dimensions are near-identical across all five, and only the weights move.

Stage changes the apparatus more than the logic. Below a few thousand growers the honest framework is a list of names to call before shipping; it becomes necessary where no single person knows who is affected — for Yashaswi, past about 400 dealers. In companies large enough to run the calendar as a budget the risk inverts: they manufacture Tier 1 candidates, because a quarter with no major launch looks like no progress.

8. Three worked examples

Seed-lot traceability: tiering that worked

The QR release reached 23,000 growers (20 per cent) with ₹145 lakh of exposure, scoring Tier 2 — but irreversibly, since 4,00,000 packs would carry printed codes. The team treated irreversibility as a gate requirement, not a tier change: a 12,000-pack pilot through 40 dealers before the full run. Scan rate came in at 31 per cent against a 25 per cent assumption, and codes on 900 pilot packs pointed to a lot record with the wrong sowing-window advisory — ₹1.8 lakh of packaging wasted rather than the print run.

Dealer credit limits: a pilot that changed the release

The credit-limit engine was the slate's largest exposure at ₹1,240 lakh. A 60-dealer pilot found the algorithm cut limits for 18 of the 60 dealers (30 per cent), which across 1,190 credit dealers meant 357 dealers facing an average reduction of ₹1.4 lakh: ₹5 crore withdrawn from the channel before sowing, 13.2 per cent of a ₹38 crore ledger. No tier of communication makes that acceptable. Limits were grandfathered for a season and reductions applied at renewal; the pilot's value was discovering that the release, as built, was wrong.

Baadal firmware 2.7: the failure and the recovery

In March 2026 Baadal shipped firmware 2.7 silently to 9,600 of the 14,800 nodes then installed (64.9 per cent); the irrigation trigger moved six points of soil moisture. There was no dealer note and no staged ring: reach-and-revenue scoring said Tier 3. Over five weeks 1,240 growers over-irrigated, 410 complained (33.1 per cent) and 610 subscriptions lapsed.

Kanchustambham put it bluntly: they had tiered by how much they were saying, when what hurt customers was what the product did on its own.

9. Failure modes, early warning, and the cost of catching them late

Announcement inflation. Early sign: a dealer broadcast every fortnight regardless of content. Diagnostic: the read-rate trend over two quarters. Caught late, the channel that carries Tier 1 news is ignored, and the next real launch lands at Tier 3 effect for Tier 1 cost.

Gate theatre. Early sign: the gate is reviewed in launch week and everything passes. Diagnostic: when did an item last fail, and what happened to the date? A gate that has never moved a date is record-keeping; the cost arrives as an outage nobody staffed for.

Silent by default for autonomous behaviour. Early sign: releases with no interface change routed automatically to Tier 3. Diagnostic: does this change what the product does when nobody is looking? Baadal's ₹39.78 lakh lesson.

One tier on a two-sided release. Early sign: a single tier field in the release template. Diagnostic: which side's base is the denominator? Caught late, one side is over-communicated and the other surprised.

Date-first tiering. Early sign: the launch date reaches a board deck before the gate is scored. Diagnostic: if the gate fails next Tuesday, who changes their plan? Caught late, commitment overrules the gate and the framework is dead for a year or more.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Position A: tiers should be a formula. Tiering exists to take the decision away from whoever is most invested, and only an auditable function of reach, exposure and reversibility resists decay into advocacy: the credit-limit pilot happened because a threshold forced it. It fails where the inputs are not measurable before release — Baadal, and every model-driven feature.

Position B: tiers are a legacy of batch release, and ramps replace them. Exposure is the only variable that matters and modern delivery sets it continuously, so a discrete tier buys nothing but meeting agendas; Baadal's own fix was a ramp. It fails where announcement is lumpy: a field-day campaign across 1,860 outlets cannot be ramped at 1 per cent.

Position C: readiness is the real gate, and tiering is downstream. Every expensive launch failure is operational rather than classificatory, and Gollapudi's decision reduces to the number 280. It fails if capacity is elastic — purchasable in a fortnight in a call-centre business, where letting the constraint set ambition permanently under-launches.

Position D: tiering is rationing and belongs in a budget. Attention is the scarce resource: allocate a fixed number of Tier 1 slots a year, make managers bid, and the trade-off becomes explicit. It fails in a year whose slate genuinely holds five major items, and this camp has no answer to that.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied tiering assigns a tier, fills the checklist and reports green. Someone who has internalised it sets tier and gate in separate meetings with different people, because the two conversations corrupt each other; quotes the constraint rather than the label — "280 escalations a week", not "Tier 1 with phasing"; names the assumption the model is most sensitive to before anyone asks; and treats a release with no visible change as a candidate for the most careful handling, not the least.

12. What each of them decided

Gollapudi kept the thrips advisory at Tier 1 and phased it over twelve weeks in three waves, ordered by sowing date rather than account value, accepting 38 per cent adoption rather than 45 and a net of ₹11.44 lakh rather than a theoretical ₹28.46 lakh. Her reason was not the ₹0.72 lakh by which phasing beat Tier 2; it was that phasing was the only option whose load — 262.2 escalations a week against 280 of headroom — she could defend to Tallapaneni's agronomists. She also commissioned a measurement of the dealer-enablement adoption lift, since the ranking stayed undefendable until somebody knew that number.

Kanchustambham did not ship firmware 3.2 in June. He shipped to a ring of 1,000 connected nodes with a 96-hour hold and a dealer briefing, treating a release with no visible change as Tier 1 on reversibility alone, and put the rest of the fleet behind connectivity remediation — because a gate score of 64 failing on rollback reach is an architecture problem, not a scheduling one.

  1. Yashaswi's framework gave the right tier to the release it scored and none at all to Baadal's. Is the defect in the thresholds, in the axes, or in expecting one framework to serve both a commerce platform and a device fleet?
  2. Exhibit 2 ranks phased Tier 1 above Tier 2 by ₹0.72 lakh, on an adoption assumption never measured. What should Gollapudi tell a board that asks whether the model justifies her decision?
  3. Kanchustambham's gate fails on a dimension he cannot improve this season. Should a gate block a release indefinitely, and if not, who overrules it, on what record?

13. Going deeper

Launch planning and launch mistakes — tiers size the plan; this is the plan.

Support and operational readiness — the origin of the number 280.

Launch readiness reviews — where tier and gate are argued by product, sales, engineering and legal.

What a GTM strategy is — tiers allocate attention within a strategy.

Your first 100 users — the stage where the apparatus is rightly a name list.

Channels: paid, owned, earned — earned channels cannot be undone.

Inbound vs outbound — decides whether a launch can be ramped: Position B's argument.

Product-led growth — pushes tiering toward in-product surfaces and ramps.

Sales-led growth — pushes it toward enablement and account sequencing.

Dhaara Tracker 4.0: How Big a Launch?

A teaching case on launch tiers and launch readiness

1. Opening

On the morning of Wednesday, 14 October 2026, Harpreet Gill sat in the Ludhiana office of Ojasvi Shopfloor Systems with two documents open: a stall-booking form for the annual cycle-parts trade fair, due back with a deposit by Friday, 16 October, and a release checklist for Dhaara Tracker 4.0, which engineering promised for Monday, 2 November. The fair opened on Friday, 27 November, twenty-five days after the release. The stall alone would cost ₹9 lakh.

Gill, the founder and chief executive, had two days to decide what kind of launch 4.0 deserved. Her product head wanted the fair, the press and a full campaign. Her head of support had sent a two-line message: "We are not ready for that. Please read my sheet before you sign."

2. Company background

Ojasvi Shopfloor Systems sells Dhaara Tracker, a job-card and production-tracking tool for small manufacturers of bicycle parts and auto components. Its customers are the forging, machining and chain-and-hub shops that supply the Ludhiana cycle cluster, home to firms such as Hero Cycles and Avon Cycles, and the Tier-2 vendors who feed Maruti Suzuki and Mahindra plants. A shop owner or floor supervisor scans a barcode on a job card at each machine; the tool shows what is running, what is late and how long each operation actually took. Most customers previously used paper cards and Tally Prime.

The company has 310 paying customers at an average of ₹1.8 lakh a year, an annual recurring revenue of 558 lakh, or ₹5.58 crore. Most are Udyam-registered MSMEs in Ludhiana, Jalandhar and Phagwara. Zoho offers general tools that a shop must configure for itself, SAP Business One is priced for larger plants, and a Delhi start-up sells a lighter tracker with weaker offline support. Word of mouth among owners has been Ojasvi's best channel. Its support team of five is small, and that fact drives the case.

3. The situation

Version 4.0 bundles two features. The first is a Rework and Scrap Ledger, which records every rejected piece and the machine and shift that produced it. Every one of the 310 customers could use it, and Ojasvi plans to sell it as an add-on at ₹0.5 lakh a year. The second is an OEM Quality Report, which formats inspection data the way large auto buyers ask for it. It is relevant to the 84 customers who supply Tier-1 auto firms, at ₹1.2 lakh a year. Beyond these, the sales pipeline holds 60 prospects, and the team believes about 36 could sign at the standard ₹1.8 lakh if the release is promoted well.

Navneet Grewal, the head of product, sees the fair as the moment of the year. Every owner in the cluster walks the aisles, and a strong Tier 1 launch would announce that Ojasvi is more than a tracker. Option B: Tier 2, targeted launch. Release on 2 November to the existing base and the 60 prospects, through webinars, videos and visits by Bajwa's team. Skip the stall. Expected revenue is ₹106.8 lakh for ₹8 lakh, within support capacity. The cost is visibility, and Grewal's stage.

Option C: Tier 3, release notes only. Switch features on with an in-app message. 7. Questions for discussion

  1. What separates a release from a launch at Ojasvi, and which parts of 4.0 are genuinely launch-worthy?
  2. Why does Exhibit 2 rank the tiers differently by absolute return and by return per rupee spent? Which reading should Gill weigh more, and why?
  3. Using Exhibit 3, which gates determine the maximum tier available on 2 November? Which can be closed by then, and which cannot?

8. A note for the learner

How the topic frames the decision. A launch tier sizes the effort to the impact, and readiness sets a ceiling on the tier. The question is not "how much can we earn from a large launch?" but "how large a launch can we serve without breaking what we already have?" Exhibit 2 answers the first question in favour of Tier 1 and the second in favour of Tier 2.

Spend the ₹8 lakh, and start hiring the three agents today so that capacity for 57 onboardings a month exists by late December. Treat the sync fix on 30 October as a hard gate: if it slips again, delay the release by a week rather than onboard customers onto tablets that lose data. Return to a Tier 1 launch, once support capacity and the sync fix have both been demonstrated.

The reasoning is that Tier 2 captures ₹106.8 lakh of the ₹161.7 lakh, about 66 per cent, at 36 per cent of the cost, and protects the reputation for reliability that supplies the company's word-of-mouth. The cost, delayed visibility, is recoverable; a failed onboarding wave among 310 trusting customers would not be. A good answer names this asymmetry and states what it gives up.
