Kinaara Cold Chain Systems: What Tier Is a Catch Certificate?

Launch tiers and launch readiness. Karwar, January 2027.

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on Sunday, 17 January 2027, the generator at the Karwar fishing harbour was still running and Dhanya Karkera could hear it from her flat above the office. On her screen were two versions of the same forecast for the same release, produced three weeks apart by two of her own colleagues, differing by ₹166.2 lakh. Beside the laptop lay a note from her chair, asking her to bring a recommendation to Monday's three o'clock board call: which of three launch tiers Kinaara Cold Chain Systems would run for version 4.0, and what it would cost.

She had spent the weekend on that question and arrived at a different one. Every input to the tier decision, she had begun to suspect, was an artefact of something else: of how sales counted customers, of which month you asked about capacity, of a clause signed in 2023, and of a European audit calendar nobody in Karwar controlled. The tier framework had been her idea. She was no longer sure it was a framework at all.

2. The company, and one clause from 2023

Kinaara was founded in Karwar in 2019 on a narrow problem: a carton of frozen shrimp leaving a Karnataka freezing plant carried a paper trail that could not survive a buyer's audit. Its product, Yugma Lot Trace, sits between the landing centre and the export invoice. A harbour clerk records vessel, trip and landing; the peeling shed records yield; the cold store records temperature; and the documentation desk pulls a lot genealogy for each consignment. The alternative was a register, a weighing slip and Tally Prime.

By January 2027 the product was live at 312 sites from Ratnagiri to Kollam, billed to 61 contracting entities, at annual recurring revenue of ₹678.8 lakh, or ₹6.788 crore. Those three numbers describe one company and are used interchangeably inside it, which is the first thing to distrust.

In November 2023, when ARR was ₹126 lakh, Karkera signed an enterprise agreement with Rangoli Marine Exports, a Bhatkal group with plants, peeling sheds and cold stores across three states. Rangoli paid a flat ₹38 lakh a year — then 30.2 per cent of ARR, now 5.6 per cent — and the agreement runs to 31 March 2029. Clause 7.2, drafted by Rangoli's counsel and not contested by Kinaara's, covered "all modules, features and successor versions of the Licensed Software, at all Units of the Group whether presently operated or hereafter acquired, at no additional charge." At the time it bought survival. Rangoli now operates 96 of the 312 connected sites, 30.8 per cent of them.

3. The industry

India's marine exports are governed by authorities the product must satisfy without being paid by any of them. The Marine Products Export Development Authority registers exporters and packing units; the Export Inspection Agency, under the Export Inspection Council, approves establishments for the European Union and issues health certificates; the FSSAI governs domestic food safety; and the European Commission audits India's control system, using the catch certificate and the establishment approval list. Certification is not a feature. It is the condition of the trade.

The competition is uneven. Large groups run in-house software or spreadsheets; SAP and Zoho appear in tenders and rarely convert at this size. The real threat is Chhaya Dockside, a Kochi firm two years younger and documentation-first: less shop-floor capture, faster certificate output, and an aggressive presence at MPEDA's buyer-seller meets. Downstream the buyer side is consolidating, and it is the importer, not the regulator, who usually sets the date.

4. The situation in detail

Version 4.0 bundles three components as the Catch Certificate Pack. Lot Genealogy, ₹0.9 lakh a unit a year, links each export carton back to vessel and trip. The EU Catch Certificate module, ₹2.4 lakh, produces the European format and its electronic payload, and is meaningful only at the 104 sites holding EU establishment approval. The audit-grade Cold-store Temperature Log, ₹0.6 lakh, suits the 190 sites with their own cold storage. New pipeline units pay the standard ₹3.6 lakh licence.

The sequence of belief matters more than the sequence of events. On 12 October 2026 the European Commission notified an audit mission to India for 8 to 19 February 2027; the team read this as a deadline and a marketing opportunity at once. On 20 November a field trial at Honnavar failed in a way nobody had modelled: the jetty has no usable data connection at four in the morning, and the offline queue silently dropped lots when the tablet battery died. Engineering committed to a fix by 5 February 2027, seventy-seven days, or eleven weeks, later. On 14 December sales published Exhibit 2, built on connected sites. On 6 January, preparing the board pack, finance and customer success rebuilt it on billable units as Exhibit 3. On 15 January Rangoli's importer in Vigo wrote that its supplier portal moves to schema version 3 on 1 March 2027, frozen on 12 February, and that suppliers not submitting genealogy in the new format from that date would go to manual inspection.

That letter changed the arithmetic of every tier without changing a figure in the tier table. Rangoli has 96 units, pays nothing further for them under clause 7.2, and now has a commercial reason to demand all of them live inside six weeks.

Dhanya Karkera, founder and chief executive, Karwar. She built the company on the claim that Kinaara never breaks a harbour's routine. She designed the tier framework last year and is now the only person who doubts it. She has not told the board that she signed clause 7.2 herself.

Ravindra Salian, head of product, Bengaluru. He wants Tier 1 and the MPEDA platform: the February audit mission is a once-in-five-years reason to be the name attached to the catch certificate before Chhaya Dockside is. His incentive is a module launch on his record. What he is not saying is that the 5 February offline fix has a known gap — it does not cover the hand-held weighing scales used at two of the four harbours.

Kishore Kotian, head of customer success, Honnavar. Six people report to him. He has said in writing that he can absorb "about forty activations a month", and privately knows the figure came from a good March. He wants the smallest possible launch, and also three hires, which a small launch will not justify.

Renuka Puthran, chief financial officer, Chennai. She built Exhibit 3 and defends it. She has not circulated the sensitivity in which the Rangoli units, being contractually free, are stripped out of revenue but left in the load; she intends to raise it herself at the board call.

Launch Tiers and Launch Readiness

How big a launch does this release deserve?

Tuesday morning, Amritsar

On the morning of 6 October 2026, Karanvir Sandhu, vice president of product at Rachna Legal Cloud, opened a spreadsheet he had been avoiding for a week. Rachna sold contract-lifecycle and legal-operations software — clause libraries, approval workflows, obligation tracking, e-stamping and e-signature integration, vendor and NDA repositories — to 1,200 mid-market companies across India, from an office two kilometres from the Golden Temple. Average annual contract value across the base was roughly ₹4.5 lakh, putting total recurring revenue near ₹54 crore. Two releases were scheduled for 20 October, three weeks before the mid-November wave of renewals Rachna's finance team called Diwali season.

The first release let a contract route through sign-off chains across multiple legal entities — promised to exporters and holding companies for a year. The second was a small convenience: saved filters on the clause-library search screen. Both were done and tested; Karanvir's problem was how loudly to ship each, with a support desk of four engineers already at 85 percent capacity. Launch the multi-entity feature too quietly and it sits undiscovered through the one window each year when customers decide whether to renew and upgrade. Launch it too loudly, too soon, and the support queue seizes up in the exact three weeks account managers need clear for renewal calls.

The idea: sizing the launch to the release

A launch tier is a pre-agreed classification of how much coordinated effort — announcement, documentation, sales enablement, support staffing, rollback planning — a release deserves, decided by how many customers it touches and how much rides on it working, not by how many engineer-hours built it. The practice spread through SaaS product organisations in the second half of the 2010s, as companies grew from a few dozen customers, where a founder could message everyone personally, to thousands, where treating a font-size tweak and a core-engine change identically either buried the important release in noise or exhausted customers over a trivial one. Tiering separates "is this release finished?" — an engineering judgement — from "how much does the world need to be told, and are we ready to be told back?" — a go-to-market judgement. The sentence Karanvir could say without sounding glib: we size the launch to the release, not the release to the launch. A Tier 1 rollout is not a reward for effort spent building it, and a quiet Tier 3 release is not a verdict that the work didn't matter.

How the tiering decision actually gets made

The assignment runs in five steps, and the first two are usually done from memory rather than a spreadsheet — which is where teams get it wrong. Step one is estimating reach: what fraction of the active base will have its workflow touched, not what fraction merely could use the feature. Step two is estimating impact — revenue at stake, either upside ARR from upgrades or downside risk to renewals. Step three, an axis practitioners often collapse into impact but should not, is change risk: whether the release alters behaviour customers already rely on, or is purely additive. Modest reach and modest revenue can still demand careful handling if change risk is high — precisely why regulated flows such as e-stamping and digital-signature integration get special treatment. Step four scores reach and impact against agreed thresholds to land on Tier 1, 2 or 3. Step five — most often skipped — runs that assignment through a readiness gate: a checklist, independent of tier size, that must clear before the tier's launch machinery fires. A release can score Tier 1 by the numbers and still be blocked if the support runbook isn't written, battlecards aren't ready, or legal sign-off on a statutory workflow hasn't landed. The gate is not a formality bolted on after the tier is decided; it is what stops an under-prepared team from shipping enthusiasm it cannot support.

Fig. 1 — Reach and revenue at stake place a release in one of three tiers; change risk (not shown) can push a low-reach, compliance-touching release upward regardless of where it lands here.

Working the numbers Karanvir actually had

Multi-entity approval routing touched only the segment of Rachna's base with more than one legal entity — exporters, holding companies, group structures — 25 percent of the 1,200-customer base, or 300 companies. Rachna priced the capability as an add-on averaging ₹60,000 in incremental annual revenue per upgrading customer, so the total upside was 300 times ₹60,000: ₹1,80,00,000, or ₹1.8 crore. Both Tier 1 criteria cleared — reach above 20 percent, revenue above ₹1 crore. By the scoring alone, this was a Tier 1 release.

The readiness gate told a different story. Rachna's checklist held eight standing items — release notes, changelog, help-centre article, support runbook, support staffing plan, sales battlecards, customer email, and legal sign-off on the e-stamp vendor's multi-entity certificate handling. Five were done; three were not — staffing plan, battlecards, and a Punjabi-language help article regional customers had asked for. Five of eight sits below Rachna's own six-of-eight threshold for a full Tier 1 launch.

The arithmetic explained the threshold. Four support engineers handled 40 tickets each per week — 160 combined. At 85 percent utilisation they already absorbed 136 a week, leaving headroom of 24. Rachna's last two Tier 1 launches ran roughly 14 tickets per 100 active users touching a changed workflow in the first month. All 300 customers at once, three users each, meant 900 users and 126 tickets — about 63 a week over two weeks, 39 above headroom, enough to drown support in the exact weeks account managers needed it clear.

Karanvir's second pass changed one input: a first wave of 100 customers — one-third of the segment, nearest renewal dates first — instead of all 300. That produced 300 users, 42 tickets over two weeks, 21 a week: three inside the 24-ticket headroom, a thin but real margin. Revenue still reconciled: 100 customers at ₹60,000 was ₹60,00,000 in wave-one upside, with the remaining 200 — ₹1,20,00,000, or ₹1.2 crore — following once the three gate items closed, together still totalling ₹1.8 crore.

Table 1 — Two releases, two tier outcomes

Seven distinctions worth becoming precise about

Tier is not a scoreboard for engineering effort

A three-month rebuild of the routing engine's internals can still be Tier 3 if customer-facing behaviour is unchanged; a one-line pricing-page fix can be Tier 1 if it touches every visitor's first impression. Reach and revenue decide the tier, not sprints spent building it.

Tier is not the same as internal priority

A release can be P0 on the roadmap, blocking three enterprise deals, and still be Tier 3 for launch purposes — "important to the business" and "needs a customer-facing announcement" answer different questions.

The readiness gate can override the scoring, never the other way round

A release qualifying for Tier 1 by reach and revenue cannot be waved through if support or sales enablement isn't ready — the gate is a hard stop. A low-scoring release is not promoted to Tier 1 just because the gate is ready early; readiness is necessary, not sufficient.

"Silent" does not mean undocumented

Tier 3 removes the proactive push — no email, no webinar, no battlecard — but the changelog and help article still ship, because a support agent should never be the one first telling a customer something changed.

Compliance-touching changes carry a floor tier regardless of reach

A change to how signed documents route to an e-stamping partner can affect four customers and still deserve support staffing and legal sign-off, because a broken compliance flow is legal exposure, not a support ticket. Rachna's checklist encoded this as a mandatory line, evaluated before the reach score.

Tier can drift downward across a release's own follow-on patches

Once a feature ships Tier 1, a bug-fix patch riding on it inherits a lower tier by default because its own reach looks small — usually right, but a team must recheck reach whenever the patch itself changes behaviour further.

Marketing enthusiasm is a bias to name, not to deny

Sales and marketing have a structural reason to want every release scored Tier 1 — it gives them content to send — which is exactly why scoring must happen against written thresholds before the marketing calendar is drafted, not after.

Consumer, B2B and marketplace — and early-stage versus large company

Rachna is B2B, so reach is counted in accounts and revenue is tied to named-account renewal dates — why Karanvir could compute an exact rupee figure at all. A consumer product measures reach in daily active users and carries a risk B2B mostly avoids: a "silent" Tier 3 change can spread through screenshots faster than any planned announcement. A marketplace has to ask reach twice: a change to how vendors upload NDA templates may be Tier 1 for the supply side and invisible to demand-side drafters, and the two sides can legitimately land in different tiers from the same release. Stage matters as much as product type. At forty customers, "20 percent reach" is eight accounts a founder can call personally — the formal apparatus is overkill, replaced by asking "who do I need to tell before this ships." Past a few hundred accounts, as at Rachna, informal judgement stops scaling, and the written framework exists to stop every team deciding importance on its own.

Common mistakes

Every release gets the same size of announcement

Symptom: a product-update email lands every two weeks regardless of content. Misunderstanding: treating "shipped" as a synonym for "significant." Diagnostic: watch the unsubscribe rate on those emails climb over a quarter.

Engineering-ready is mistaken for launch-ready

Symptom: a high-reach release ships quietly once code passes tests, then support is blindsided by ticket volume. Misunderstanding: assuming tests passing and a support runbook existing are the same milestone. Diagnostic: ask the support lead "did you see this before it shipped" — if no, the gate was skipped.

A compliance-adjacent change ships as Tier 3 because reach was small

Symptom: a regulatory complaint surfaces weeks later, traced to a routing change nobody flagged. Misunderstanding: applying the ordinary reach-and-revenue score to a release that should have tripped a separate floor. Diagnostic: a standing checklist line — does this touch e-stamping, e-signature or a statutory workflow — checked before the reach number is even calculated.

The tier is set by whoever argues loudest, not by the score

Symptom: the launch tier shifts depending on which team is in the room that week. Misunderstanding: treating tier assignment as negotiation rather than computation against written thresholds. Diagnostic: was the tier decided before or after the marketing calendar — if after, it was likely reverse-engineered.

Fig. 2 — Rachna's readiness gate blocked a full Tier 1 launch on the original date; phasing the wave, not lowering the tier, closed the gap.

What good looks like

Three months later, when Rachna extended e-signature workflows to board resolutions, the same team ran the process the way it should have run the first time. Reach and revenue were scored in the planning meeting, before any marketing calendar existed. The readiness gate was checked two weeks ahead of the target date, and every item closed on schedule, including a compliance sign-off requested from the e-sign vendor a full month early rather than the week before. Karanvir ran one cross-functional session — product, support, sales and legal together, each rehearsing the questions their own customers would ask — instead of four separate briefings that half-agreed with each other. The launch still phased its rollout, not because the gate had failed, but because phasing had simply become the default for anything touching more than a fifth of the base. Nothing about it was quieter than it needed to be, and nothing was louder than support could absorb.

"We size the launch to the release, not the release to the launch."

What Karanvir decided

Karanvir kept the multi-entity feature at Tier 1 by classification but phased its rollout: a first wave of 100 customers, nearest renewal dates first, went live on 20 October with full release notes, changelog and customer email, while staffing, battlecards and the Punjabi help article were finished over the next three weeks. The remaining 200 followed on 10 November, ahead of the renewal peak, once the gate read 8 of 8. Saved filters shipped the same day as Tier 3 — a changelog line and nothing else, the right amount of attention for a feature 96 percent of the base would never notice. Two questions to sit with: when your scoring says a release deserves a major launch but your checklist says you aren't ready, which do you trust — and is there a release on your own roadmap sized by how hard it was to build, rather than by how many customers are about to feel it?

Choosing the GTM Motion

Given a deal's size and its buyer, which go-to-market motion can a company actually afford to run — and how does the answer change as the same company grows?

1 · A board slide with two rows that do not add up

On the second Tuesday of November 2026, Meera Nambiar, VP of Product and Growth at Elaan Kitchen Systems, stood before her board with a slide she had rewritten four times. Elaan sold software to restaurants and cloud kitchens out of Madurai — a point-of-sale and kitchen-display system that throttled incoming orders when a kitchen was overloaded and kept menus and prices in sync across every aggregator a restaurant listed on. The company had grown to 1,462 paying accounts and ₹30.74 crore in annual recurring revenue, and the board wanted to know how the next ₹15 crore would be won.

The trouble was that Elaan's revenue was really three businesses wearing one logo. Single-outlet cloud kitchens signed up for ₹15,000 a month and rarely spoke to a human before paying. Chains with three to eight outlets wanted a call confirming the throttling logic would survive a Friday-night rush and how menus synced to Zomato and Swiggy. Chains of nine outlets or more needed months of procurement, a custom aggregator integration, and a CFO's signature. Her sales head wanted six new enterprise account executives, at ₹42 lakh fully loaded each, to chase big chains harder; her growth lead wanted the same money spent on self-serve onboarding for kitchens Elaan had never spoken to. Both could point to a segment where their approach worked; neither had shown the arithmetic for why. Get the choice wrong, and Elaan either starves the segment that converts or builds a sales force that spends more closing a deal than it is worth — and Meera had one slide and eleven minutes to make the case.

2 · The idea, defined precisely

A go-to-market motion is the mechanism a company relies on to move a prospective customer from first contact to a signed contract — who does the convincing, how much human effort it costs per deal, and how long it takes. The two poles are product-led growth (PLG), where the product itself convinces through a free trial or freemium tier and a human joins only after the customer has found value, and sales-led growth (SLG), where a salesperson, often with a solutions engineer, drives the deal from first call to signature. Between them sits a family of hybrid motions, usually called sales-assisted PLG, where the product still does most of the early work but a person steps in for a demo, a pricing conversation, or a migration.

Product-led growth was popularised around 2016 by Blake Bartlett and colleagues at OpenView Venture Partners, watching companies like Slack and Dropbox grow revenue without a traditional sales force and needing a name for it. Sales-led growth is older than any label; it is the enterprise sales model business software has used since the mainframe era, and it never left deals that need a human to navigate a buying committee. The sentence Meera could say in the boardroom without sounding glib was this: the GTM motion is not a philosophy a company picks, it is a constraint deal size and buyer impose on it, and mismatching the two burns cash whichever direction the mismatch runs.

3 · How the match actually gets made

Practitioners talk as if deal size were the only variable, and it is the one that shows up in every slide, but three things move together. The first is deal size, usually measured as annual contract value (ACV) — how much one signed customer is worth in a year. The second is buyer complexity — whether the decision is one person with a credit card or a committee including finance, IT and legal. The third, most often left implicit, is product complexity — how much configuration or integration a customer needs before the product delivers value, independent of price.

The mechanics, once past the labels: estimate the segment's ACV; estimate the fully loaded cost of acquiring one customer, including rep, solutions-engineer and onboarding time; divide the second by the first for CAC as a share of first-year revenue; compare against a threshold finance will defend. Elaan's was 25 per cent — above that, the motion quietly subsidises growth out of gross margin, and the subsidy cannot scale past a certain deal volume.

4 · The arithmetic, worked twice

Meera ran the numbers for all three segments using the same sales-led motion — two discovery calls and one solutions-engineering session — because that was what her sales head proposed to extend everywhere. Finance had already costed one such cycle, including rep time, solutions-engineer time and onboarding, at ₹75,000 regardless of segment, since the calls take roughly the same effort whoever is on the other end.

The single-outlet segment failed badly: a sales-led motion would spend 41.7 per cent of first-year revenue just to sign one, confirming the growth lead was right that this segment needs a different motion. Self-serve signup, in-app onboarding and a usage-based upgrade nudge dropped acquisition cost there to roughly ₹8,000 — 4.4 per cent of ACV — because the product, not a person, did the convincing. Enterprise passed sales-led economics easily at 10.4 per cent, confirming the sales head's instinct for big chains was sound on its own terms. Mid-market sat exactly on the 25 per cent line — not obviously PLG or SLG — and needed the hybrid motion, a single confirmatory call replacing the full two-call cycle, costed at ₹30,000 and bringing CAC down to 10.0 per cent, affordable without pretending an eight-kitchen chain could be won with no human contact.

The second pass showed why the table cannot be frozen once computed. Enterprise ACV assumed twelve outlets per signed chain; rerun on newer wins averaging six outlets, ACV fell to ₹3.6 lakh and CAC-to-ACV doubled, from 10.4 to 20.8 per cent. Still affordable, but only just — outlets-per-account, untracked until then, was quietly deciding whether the motion kept paying for itself.

5 · What a learner has to become aware of

The threshold is a judgement, not a law

Twenty-five per cent was Elaan's own number, chosen for its margin and appetite for subsidising early deals. A company with thinner margins, or deliberately buying share, draws the line elsewhere; the framework says compute the ratio, not what ratio is acceptable.

Deal size and buyer complexity are different axes

A single-owner chain of fifteen outlets can be a bigger deal than a nine-outlet franchise-trust chain, yet have one decision-maker instead of a committee. Collapsing both into "big deal, therefore sales-led" misses cases a bigger self-serve plan could serve.

Product complexity can override a favourable ACV

If the aggregator integration needs a week of engineering time regardless of outlet count, even a modest deal may need a human to shepherd it, because the product cannot deliver value unassisted no matter how simple the buyer is.

PLG is not "free trial with a salesperson standing by"

A trial a rep calls about on day two is sales-led with a discount. Genuine PLG means most prospects who convert never speak to Elaan at all.

The motion is a channel decision, not a pricing decision

How a customer is acquired and how they are priced are related but separate; a usage-priced product can sell entirely sales-led, and a flat-fee one entirely self-serve. Confusing the two sends teams to redesign pricing when the real problem is acquisition.

The mix inside a segment can drift under a fixed motion

Section 4 showed outlets-per-deal moving from twelve to six nearly doubled CAC as a share of ACV with no motion change at all; the ratio needs recomputing periodically, not filing away once.

What the framework cannot tell you

It says nothing about whether the product retains the customer, whether the market is large enough to matter, or whether a rival's faster motion makes an affordable one uncompetitive on speed. It answers only "can we afford this," never "should we."

The question a newcomer should ask first

What is inside the CAC number — onboarding, ninety-day support, the cost of deals that never close? A ratio built on rep salary alone always looks more affordable than it is.

6 · How the picture changes by product type and by company stage

In consumer software, buyer and user are almost always the same person, so buyer complexity rarely binds; deal size and product complexity do the work, which is why consumer apps default to PLG. In B2B software like Elaan's, buyer and user are often different people even within one restaurant, and the committee grows with the organisation, so B2B leans on buyer complexity far more. Marketplace products often run two motions at once, one per side, that rarely match — a food-aggregator might onboard restaurants sales-assisted while acquiring diners through pure product-led loops.

Stage matters as much as category. An early-stage company usually cannot afford a motion per segment; it picks the one its founders run best and takes whatever deals fit, imperfectly. A company at Elaan's stage, with three visible segments and enough volume in each, can afford Table 1's analysis and run three motions at once. A large, mature company often inherits a legacy motion from when every deal needed a human, and the harder problem becomes migrating a segment to a cheaper one without the sales organisation reading it as a threat to headcount.

7 · Common mistakes

Chasing the fashionable motion. Symptom: a company adopts self-serve signup because competitors did, then quietly restaffs support with de facto salespeople on every call. Error: copying a motion without checking whether the buyer and product complexity that made it work elsewhere are present here. Diagnostic: Table 1's ratio, run on the company's own CAC, not a borrowed benchmark.

Running one motion across a widening segment spread. Symptom: reps closing tiny deals while self-serve fails to convert large chains. Error: treating "our customers" as one segment instead of three. Diagnostic: plot ACV against buyer complexity for the last hundred closed deals, as Figure 1 does.

Costing the motion on rep salary alone. Symptom: a CAC-to-ACV ratio safely under threshold while margins quietly erode. Error: excluding onboarding, early support and lost-deal cost from CAC. Diagnostic: ask finance for fully loaded cost per closed deal, not cost per booked meeting.

Freezing the motion once chosen. Symptom: a segment affordable eighteen months ago is now quietly unprofitable, found only at the next board review. Error: treating the ratio as decided once rather than recomputed as mix shifts. Diagnostic: track deal size and outlets-per-account per segment every quarter, as Elaan's second pass forced it to.

8 · What good looks like

Ezhil Cloud Kitchens, a smaller rival Meera studied before the board meeting, had made the same three-segment split two years earlier under its founder, Ramesh Sundaram. Its single-outlet tier ran entirely on self-serve signup, support answering onboarding questions, not sales. Its mid-market tier used one thirty-minute call per prospect, scripted tightly enough for any account manager to run. Its enterprise tier employed two account executives, each measured on CAC-to-ACV per deal, reviewed quarterly against threshold. When Ezhil's average enterprise outlet count fell, as Elaan's had, finance flagged it within a quarter, not a year, because outlets-per-account was already a tracked metric, not a number reconstructed under board pressure.

9 · What Meera decided

Meera recommended, and the board approved, a motion per segment rather than one motion for the company: self-serve PLG for single-outlet kitchens, hybrid sales-assisted PLG for the three-to-eight-outlet mid-market, and the full sales-led motion, with the six new account executives, reserved for chains of nine outlets or more. She added one condition the sales head had not asked for: outlets-per-account, alongside ACV, would be reported every quarter for enterprise specifically, because Section 4's second pass had shown that number alone could nearly double the motion's CAC-to-ACV ratio and close in on the 25 per cent threshold without a single meeting noticing. The next question Elaan's leadership took up was what happens when one large customer starts inside the self-serve tier and grows into enterprise territory while still served by the wrong motion — running more than one motion on the same account, rather than one motion per segment of accounts.

Two questions worth sitting with:
  • If your own product's CAC figure excluded onboarding cost, how much would that flatter the ratio you use to decide who gets a salesperson?
  • What is the leading indicator inside your best-performing segment today that, if it drifted quietly for a year, would turn an affordable motion into an unaffordable one before anyone noticed?

Elaan Kitchen Systems and Ezhil Cloud Kitchens are illustrative companies constructed for this case; Zomato and Swiggy are named only as real aggregator platforms restaurants commonly integrate with.

Raasta Kitchen Ledger: Choosing the GTM Motion

A teaching case in Go-to-Market and Launch

1. Opening

On the evening of Tuesday 6 October 2026, Bhakti Prabhudesai sat in the first-floor office of Raasta Kitchen Ledger in Panaji, with the Mandovi visible beyond the window and a single line on her screen: "Board, 14 October: GTM plan for the multi-outlet module." The Goa tourist season was about to start, Diwali was five weeks away, and restaurant groups across India were about to enter their busiest ordering quarter. The board had told her that incremental go-to-market spending for the next twelve months could not exceed ₹40 lakh. She had to choose how Raasta would sell to restaurant chains, and she had eight days to do it.

2. Company background

Raasta was founded in 2019 by Prabhudesai and a former restaurant manager from Margao. It sells software that tells a kitchen what each plate really costs. The product has three parts: recipe costing, food-cost variance tracking against purchases, and ordering from suppliers across several outlets. Its first customers were cloud kitchens, small delivery-only operations that list on Zomato and Swiggy, where a two-point slip in food cost decides whether an outlet earns anything at all.

The company grew almost entirely by self-service. A kitchen owner signed up on the website, uploaded a menu, and paid ₹1,500 a month by UPI, with no salesperson involved. Raasta issues GST-compliant purchase records and reads supplier invoices, which owners valued. Competitors included point-of-sale vendors such as Petpooja that bundle inventory features, and spreadsheets, still the largest rival. Large multi-brand operators are the market's upper end, and Raasta had never pursued them.

By September 2026 Raasta had 1,674 paying customers and annual recurring revenue (ARR) of ₹5.70 crore (Exhibit 1). The team was 41 people: product and engineering in Margao, a support and implementation desk in Vasco, and a few remote members.

3. The situation

The chains were an accident. Fourteen had signed over thirty months, mostly through the founders' contacts, and together they produced ₹84 lakh, or 14.7 per cent of ARR from 0.8 per cent of customers. Each paid about ₹6 lakh a year. They also asked for things a single kitchen never did: bulk menu and recipe imports across 30 outlets, approval levels for purchase orders, and a regional manager's view of variance.

Product managers had built a multi-outlet module in response, and in the past twelve months 30 qualified chain trials had started, almost all from inbound interest. Exhibit 2 shows what happened to them. Twelve completed a bulk import, six ran multi-outlet ordering for two weeks, and three signed. The trial software worked; the loss came from the setup, when a chain's operations head had to map hundreds of ingredients to supplier items with nobody to ask.

Around the table, the team saw the situation from different places (Exhibit 3). Oorja Dessai, the customer-success lead in Singapore, ran onboarding calls for the chains at her own evening hours. She reported that a typical chain needed eleven working days and four calls to finish setup, and that four chains had told her the same thing: "We will pay, but someone has to sit with us." Umesh Sardesai, the sales head in New Jersey, had come from an enterprise software firm and pointed out that Raasta's largest prospect had budgets of crores. He wanted field reps in Hyderabad, Mumbai and Delhi. Ira Shirodkar, the head of product in Margao, feared that any sales-led effort would pull engineers into custom work for individual chains.

Exhibit 3: Where the four decision-makers sit. Singapore is 2.5 hours ahead of India; New Jersey is 9.5 hours behind it in October.

4. The people

Bhakti Prabhudesai, CEO, Panaji, holds the decision and wants growth that does not exhaust the ₹40 lakh ceiling. Umesh Sardesai, sales head, New Jersey, wants a field team and believes chains will not be won by web forms. Ira Shirodkar, head of product, Margao, wants the product to remain self-explaining and the roadmap free of one-off requests. Oorja Dessai, customer-success lead, Singapore, wants a person assigned to every chain's first month, and has the ticket data to support it.

A live opportunity sharpened the debate. Chayan Bhojanalaya Group, a 30-outlet chain with kitchens in Hyderabad and Bengaluru, had asked for a paid pilot and a named contact. Its operations head told Oorja it would decide before Diwali stock orders went out.

5. The options

Option A: stay self-serve. Spend ₹12 lakh on onboarding content, in-app guides and trial credits (₹7 lakh plus ₹5 lakh). The cost is small and the motion is proven, but the funnel in Exhibit 2 says it will win about three chains a year.

Option B: build a field sales team. Three field reps at ₹22 lakh each (₹66 lakh), a presales engineer at ₹18 lakh, and ₹12 lakh for travel and events, for ₹96 lakh in all. With outbound added, 40 leads a year should yield eight chains. It exceeds the board's ceiling by ₹56 lakh, and it is the motion Umesh recommends.

Option C: sales-assisted onboarding. One account executive who also does solution design in Panaji (₹18 lakh), one implementation specialist in Vasco (₹8 lakh), and ₹10 lakh for pilot support, for ₹36 lakh in total. Prospects still find Raasta by themselves, but a person joins once a chain shows intent. Management expects the 30 leads to yield six chains.

Exhibit 4 shows why the choice is not simply "cheapest" or "biggest." Option A has the quickest payback but leaves most chains unserved. Option B wins the most, but moving from C to B adds ₹60 lakh of cost for two extra chains, or ₹30 lakh per additional chain, against ₹6 lakh of annual revenue from each.

6. Questions for discussion

1. What does Exhibit 2 tell you about why chains fail to convert: product, price or lack of help? What evidence would separate the three?

2. Using Exhibit 1, what do a ₹6 lakh price and a ₹40 lakh ceiling imply about the motions Raasta can afford in the chain segment?

3. Compare A and C in Exhibit 4. How much extra does each additional chain cost, and is that acceptable?

4. If you were Bhakti, what would you tell Umesh on 14 October, and what would have to change for his plan to become right?

7. A note for the learner

This case asks a single question: given the deal size and the buyer, which motion can we afford? A motion is affordable when the cost of winning a customer is comfortably below what the customer pays over a sensible period. At about ₹6 lakh a year, a chain deal can carry a person's time, but not a travelling team. Exhibit 1 shows this: single kitchens are worth ₹18,000 a year and can only be sold by the product itself, while chains are worth thirty-three times as much and can justify a human.

One defensible path is Option C. It fits the ₹40 lakh ceiling with ₹4 lakh to spare, it targets the point where trials break (setup, not interest), and its payback of 12 months is defensible. Moving from A to C adds ₹24 lakh for three more chains, or ₹8 lakh each, which a chain paying ₹6 lakh a year repays in 16 months. That is acceptable, and the extra people also let the Chayan pilot go ahead this month. Option B fails on affordability today: it costs ₹56 lakh above the ceiling and pays back in 24 months.

Option C is not a rejection of Umesh's idea. Field selling becomes affordable when deals are larger; at a cost of ₹12 lakh per chain, an 18-month payback needs a price of at least ₹8 lakh. Bhakti should therefore name a review trigger: revisit field sales when the average chain price reaches ₹8 lakh, or when the assisted team has a pipeline it cannot serve. Ira's concern is met by a rule that the assisted team configures and never asks engineering for one-off code. The single-outlet self-serve motion continues unchanged, and the chain motion is the first step toward running several motions at once.

Vikalp Bhatti Systems: Four Motions and One Budget

A teaching case in Go-to-Market and Growth. Raipur, October 2026.

1. The night before

On the night of Sunday, 11 October 2026, Lopamudra Baghel sat in the Siltara office of Vikalp Bhatti Systems, windows shut against the smell of the sponge-iron belt, reading a one-page note she had written to herself and disliked. The board met on Wednesday, 14 October. The fund that led the company's Series A had offered a bridge of ₹14 crore, and its term sheet carried two numbers: new recurring revenue of at least ₹6.00 crore in the year to 31 March 2027, and go-to-market spending of no more than ₹2.90 crore.

Four proposals sat in front of her, each described by its author as the motion the company should now commit to. Only one fitted inside the money. None, on its own author's numbers, reached ₹6.00 crore. And a note from her head of growth had quietly undermined the exhibit on which the cheapest proposal rested. Relining shutdowns across the Chhattisgarh cluster would begin the week after Dussehra; by Diwali the plants that mattered would either have let Vikalp's engineers on site or not, and the window would close until March.

2. How the company got here

Vikalp Bhatti Systems was founded in January 2019 by Baghel, an industrial engineer who had audited energy use in rolling mills, and Srijan Kashyap, an instrumentation engineer from a Bhilai re-rolling unit. Their first product was an Android application, Vikalp Log, replacing the hand-written downtime register on the kiln floor: a shift in-charge tapped a reason code when the kiln stopped and the owner got a message at night with the hours lost. It spread through the cluster's WhatsApp groups during the 2020 lockdowns.

The decision that shaped everything afterwards was taken in December 2020. To convert the first plants willing to pay properly, the founders had to get real data — kiln temperatures, blower currents, energy-meter pulses — out of equipment that mostly dated from the 1990s and had no standard control system. Rather than integrate with third-party supervisory software, Kashyap designed a ruggedised edge gateway, assembled in Bhilai, that tapped whatever signals a plant happened to have. To persuade owners to allow it, the founders promised installation and configuration free for three years.

That decision is why Vikalp wins. It is also why every sale of Vikalp Floor needs two engineers on site for nine working days; why a commissioning fee of ₹2.50 lakh, introduced only in the year to March 2025, is still waived in roughly a third of deals; and why "self-serve" means one thing for Vikalp Log, which a works manager installs from the Play Store and pays for by UPI autopay, and another for Vikalp Floor, which cannot be bought without somebody climbing a kiln.

3. The industry

Chhattisgarh holds the densest concentration of direct-reduced-iron capacity in India. Within two hours of Raipur sit several hundred sponge-iron kilns, induction furnaces and re-rolling mills, mostly family-owned units of one to four kilns, alongside the integrated works that define the landscape: SAIL's Bhilai Steel Plant, NMDC at Nagarnar, Jindal Steel and Power at Raigarh. Coal and ore prices are set elsewhere and power tariffs by the Chhattisgarh State Power Distribution Company; the only variables an owner controls are kiln availability, energy consumption and yield.

Two regulatory forces help. Designated consumers under the Bureau of Energy Efficiency's Perform, Achieve and Trade scheme must report specific energy consumption, and group finance heads dislike assembling those numbers from registers; continuous emission monitoring has accustomed plants to instrumentation they did not want. A third cuts the other way: the Digital Personal Data Protection Act has led two groups to ask why shift operators' names appear in a dashboard.

Global automation suppliers sell execution systems priced for integrated plants, not a three-kiln unit in Durg; Indian software firms sell to the steel majors through integrators; the real incumbent is a register, a weighbridge slip and an accountant's spreadsheet. Vikalp's board returns to one question: Zoho, Freshworks and Postman built enormous businesses on products customers configured themselves, so why does Vikalp need seven engineers in a van?

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

By September 2026 Vikalp had 817 paying customers and annual recurring revenue of ₹13.48 crore (Exhibit 1). Headcount was 128, of whom 7 were commissioning engineers and 9 were in sales and growth.

The company had not chosen a go-to-market motion; it had accumulated four. Self-serve carried Vikalp Log. An inside-sales desk of two, opened in 2024, called single-plant owners across Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Jharkhand and sold Vikalp Floor at ₹4.50 lakh a year. A field motion, in practice Baghel, Kashyap and the crew, pursued multi-plant groups. And since October 2024 Hochwald Kiln Technologies GmbH of Duisburg, which supplies rotary kilns to projects in India, Oman, Indonesia and Nigeria, had shipped kilns with Vikalp Floor preloaded and its own engineers installing the gateway, against a twenty per cent revenue share. Exhibit 2 sets out what each cost and produced in the year to March 2026.

In April 2026 the board pack reported a cost of acquisition of ₹8,000 per self-serve customer and asked why the company was not putting its money there. A July pack repeated it and added the field motion at ₹4.00 lakh per customer. Exhibit 3 shows how: the ₹70 lakh commissioning crew had been booked entirely to delivery, on the grounds that customers paid a commissioning fee. That year the crew commissioned 27 plants and the fee was collected on 19 of them, yielding ₹47.50 lakh, or 67.9 per cent of the crew's cost.

In late August, Yamini Sonwani, who ran growth from Bengaluru, sampled 120 of the year's Vikalp Log signups and telephoned every one. Exhibit 5 is what she found: 18 of the 120, or 15 per cent, had arrived without prior human contact. The rest had been produced by the very motions the self-serve numbers were being used to argue against.

Two things changed in September. Hochwald asked for exclusivity in its export territories, barring Vikalp from selling directly in three markets it had never entered. And Panthshala Technical Services of Bhilai, a maintenance contractor with 180 technicians servicing roughly 240 plants, proposed reselling Vikalp Floor at a thirty per cent margin, commissioning it itself and holding the customer relationship — and asked for access to the gateway's data interface.

Figure A. The December 2020 gateway choice constrained every later motion.

5. The people

Lopamudra Baghel, chief executive, Raipur, owns the decision and has told the fund she will bring one recommendation, not four. The company's advantage, she believes, is the gateway and the crew that installs it. What she has not said aloud is that the crew may also be why the company cannot grow faster, and that she does not know whether that is a sales or a product problem.

Choosing the GTM motion

Two insurance-distribution software firms in Cuttack, and the identity that decides what either can afford.

1 · Two rooms, twelve days apartThe decisions on the table

On Thursday, 3 September 2026, Snigdha Sarangi opened Darpan Insure Networks' quarterly revenue review with a table she had had rebuilt once. Darpan, founded in Cuttack in 2019, sold a broking platform: quote comparison across fourteen insurers, digital proposal and KYC, commission reconciliation and renewals. It carried 2,180 paying accounts and ₹41.96 crore of annual recurring revenue at 31 August 2026 — three businesses in one logo: 1,760 POSP firms and one-desk brokers at ₹75,000, none of whom had spoken to Darpan, 380 brokers of five to forty seats at ₹4.20 lakh, and 40 bank-channel and composite broking arms at ₹32 lakh won by two field executives.

Sourav Bhowmick, senior vice-president for revenue, wanted six more field executives; Nibedita Patnaik, the chief financial officer, wanted each motion's cost per rupee of new revenue first. Both argued from the same three numbers and reached opposite conclusions — usually a sign the numbers are not the disagreement.

Twelve days later Debasis Routray had the inverse problem. Gulmohar Agent Cloud, founded 2021, sold a mobile quoting and commission app to individual POSP agents: 45,000 registered, 10,800 of 45,000 paying, or 24 per cent, at ₹4,800 a year and ₹4.92 crore of ARR. It was self-serve by conviction, but under the IRDAI point-of-sales framework a POSP cannot transact without a sponsoring insurer or broker, and sponsors had begun buying seat blocks for whole networks. Trilochan Padhi, who ran the agency channel, had signed twenty-six agencies in a year; his slide said the channel was cheaper and faster-paying than direct. Arupa Sahoo, the growth lead, had found an error in it.

2 · The ideaLineage, and what each school will not sign

A go-to-market motion is the mechanism by which a stranger becomes a paying customer: who persuades, how much human labour each conversion consumes, how long it takes. The poles are product-led growth, where the product persuades and a human appears only after value lands, and sales-led growth, where a seller drives it to signature.

The vocabulary is recent; the problem is not. Sales-led motion is the enterprise model inherited from the mainframe era, when nobody could try the product before buying. Product-led growth acquired its name around 2016, at OpenView Venture Partners, for firms that had grown large without a sales force — and the naming turned an observation into a prescription. This topic reinstates what that skipped: motion is a cost structure a deal must carry, not a philosophy.

Three schools disagree about which variable binds. The unit-economics school, whose lineage runs through David Skok's work on capital efficiency, holds that ACV and gross margin fix how much labour a deal can fund; it signs "a ₹75,000 deal cannot carry a ₹14 lakh sales cycle" but not "a ₹32 lakh deal must be sold by a field rep." The complexity school, from the OpenView lineage, holds that the constraint is the work between signature and first value; it signs "complexity, not price, chooses the motion" but not "low ACV implies PLG." The distribution school, strongest where intermediaries are licensed, holds that whoever owns the relationship chooses; it signs "the sponsor is the real buyer" but not that unit economics beat a channel.

3 · Mechanics in depthThe identity that pins the threshold

Competent practitioners compute CAC as a share of first-year ACV and compare it against a threshold — twenty-five per cent, thirty, whatever finance defends. Experts treat the threshold as derived, because it is. Gross-margin payback is acquisition cost over monthly gross profit; writing it out gives the identity behind everything below.

payback (months) = 12 × (CAC ÷ ACV) ÷ gross margin
Equivalently: the affordable CAC-to-ACV ratio is gross margin times tolerated payback over twelve. At a ratio equal to gross margin, payback is twelve months.

That turns an argument about taste into one about two numbers the CFO already owns. Nibedita Patnaik's tolerance was nine months, so Darpan's ceiling was 55.5 per cent — double the benchmark Sourav Bhowmick had been arguing against. Gulmohar, at 68 per cent margin, could spend 51.0 per cent.

4 · When the test applies and when it misleadsThree claims

Claim one: the ACV in the denominator is stable enough to plan on. For self-serve it is: ₹75,000 is published. For field enterprise it is not, because ACV is seats times price. Rerun the field row on the last six wins, averaging twenty-two seats not thirty-two: ACV falls to ₹22 lakh, the ratio rises from 45.0 to 65.5 per cent and payback from 7.3 to 10.6 months — through the tolerance with no decision taken. For Gulmohar it fails differently: channel ACV is negotiated.

Claim two: the product can deliver value at the cost the motion assumes. Darpan's self-serve tier passes: a one-desk broker configures nothing. But commission reconciliation needs a statement format mapped per insurer per broker, nine engineering hours whoever buys — so a ₹75,000 account adding it stops being self-serve.

Claim three: the economic and the accountable buyer are the same person. Here the test misleads actively. Under the POSP framework the agent transacts on a sponsor's licence and the sponsor carries the liability, so Gulmohar's economic buyer was the agent while its accountable buyer was always the sponsor, who can forbid the product outright. A ratio computed on the agent describes a buyer who does not control the purchase.

5 · Hard edge casesTwo-sided supply and what mature firms do

Darpan's most expensive motion had no revenue attached at all. Comparison must span enough insurers to be worth buying, and each integration costs about ₹38 lakh to build and certify plus ₹6.4 lakh a year: fourteen is ₹5.32 crore one-off and ₹89.6 lakh a year. Himansu Majumdar and a colleague ran that motion, selling to insurers at an ACV of zero.

Multi-product makes the seam visible: the quote engine is self-serve, reconciliation is not. Mature firms say they run a motion per product; they actually run one per product-segment pair, with a rule about who owns the account when pairs conflict — enforced by the compensation plan, not the deck. At eight per cent of first-year ACV a field executive earns ₹2,56,000 on a ₹32 lakh deal and ₹33,600 on a ₹4.20 lakh one: three motions on one commission scheme is one motion with extra slides.

Hardware breaks the arithmetic, not the logic: Gulmohar's village-agent kit carries ₹9,800 of unrecovered tablet cost, and adding that to a ₹15,000 self-serve CAC moves payback from 3.2 months to 5.4. AI-native products move the funnel instead: a quote-explainer lifted Darpan's activation rate in test from 32 to 41 per cent, taking 27,500 sandbox starts to 11,275 activations, 2,819 qualified and 1,409 paid on the same ₹1.65 crore, plus ₹3.83 lakh of inference at ₹34 an activated account — CAC ₹11,983, payback 2.6 months. AI changes the motion through the conversion chain, not the price, which makes the choice unstable: a rival's activation gain moves your ceiling while your price stands still. Dorothea Gebhardt, of Gebhardt Versicherungssysteme GmbH, offered to white-label the engine for Gulf brokers — no CAC, and no relationship either.

6 · The nuances that separate an expert

The threshold is gross margin times patience, not a policy

The competent practitioner argues whether twenty-five or thirty per cent is the right ceiling; the expert notices there is nothing to argue about. The tell-tale sign is a firm whose gross margin moved and whose CAC threshold did not.

The counterfactual is never zero conversions

Every case for a sales motion implicitly compares it against no motion, when the honest comparison is with what self-serve would have produced on the same prospects — rarely nothing. The tell-tale sign is a CAC-per-win quoted with no conversion rate beside it.

Payback and LTV-to-CAC can point opposite ways

Trilochan Padhi's payback figures were right: a channel seat cost ₹960 against ₹1,150 direct and paid back in 4.0 months against 4.2. Arupa Sahoo's correction was that it sells at a negotiated ₹4,224, not ₹4,800, and churns twice — seat and agency both. At 84 per cent seat retention conditional on an agency retaining at 78 per cent, combined retention is 65.5 per cent and seat life 2.90 years against 3.45; lifetime gross profit is ₹8,330 against ₹11,255, so LTV-to-CAC is 8.68 against 9.79. The faster-paying motion is the less valuable one; the tell-tale sign is a channel argued in payback months alone.

Capacity binds before affordability does

Darpan's board wanted ₹15 crore of new ARR. Field supplies it: 46.875 deals at ₹32 lakh, so ten executives at ₹72 lakh, ₹7.2 crore, ₹0.48 per rupee of new ARR. Self-serve looks better at ₹0.20 — 2,000 accounts at ₹15,000 — but at a 0.4 per cent visitor-to-paid rate that needs 5,00,000 visitors against last year's 2,75,000, and the marginal visitor does not cost ₹60. At ₹86 for the extra 2,25,000, spend is ₹3.585 crore, CAC ₹17,925, payback 3.9 months — still the best motion, no longer the same number.

Cycle length is a cash-flow variable

A thirty-one-week field cycle means spend precedes revenue by seven months before payback even begins: working capital is annual cost times cycle over fifty-two, about ₹86 lakh parked against ₹144 lakh of annual spend. The tell-tale sign is a board that has approved a motion's cost but not its float.

The accountable buyer outranks the economic buyer

In IRDAI-supervised distribution the sponsor carries liability for what a POSP does, so it holds a veto no agent's card can overcome. The tell-tale sign is an uncosted compliance step inside a self-serve funnel — Gulmohar's KYC drop-off sat in the activation rate, read as a design problem.

Segment drift is invisible because it is nobody's metric

Seats per enterprise account fell from thirty-two to twenty-two with no meeting noticing, and that alone pushed field payback from 7.3 to 10.6 months: motion economics decay less often because costs rise than because the denominator shrinks. The tell-tale sign is that nobody can state trailing-six-deal ACV without opening the CRM.

A motion is a hiring decision that outlives the analysis

Self-serve spend can be halved in a week; ten field executives cannot, and the unwinding cost appears in no CAC figure. The expert weighs reversibility as well as ratio, preferring the motion that is wrong more cheaply. Pricing interacts: seat pricing invites block negotiation, which is why Gulmohar's list ACV was not its realised one.

7 · Where the differences are realProduct type and stage

The differences across product types are uneven, and worth saying where they are not real. In consumer software buyer and user coincide, so buyer complexity almost never binds and the question reduces to the Figure 1 chain. In B2B the third claim matters and the first two are shared with consumer; that is the only real difference, and it is large. In enterprise the motion is often set by the buyer's procurement calendar — who decides differs, not how to compute. Platforms carry the Figure 2 problem; hardware loads the numerator; AI moves the conversion chain, shifting the ceiling faster than planning can track.

Stage changes the question rather than the answer. An early company cannot afford a motion per segment and runs the one its founders can run personally, taking mismatched deals. At Darpan's stage three motions are affordable and the constraint is the compensation seam; at scale it is migration against a sales organisation's fear for its own headcount.

The second is Gulmohar's channel, where the inside-sales pilot is disqualified, not merely worse — CAC of ₹6,900 against ₹4,800 of ACV is 143.8 per cent and payback 25.4 months, outside the 51.0 per cent ceiling. It survived two quarters because it lifted retention to 78 per cent — a satisfying metric to improve.

9 · Failure modes and early warnings

Importing someone else's threshold. Early sign: nobody can say where the ceiling came from. Diagnostic: do our gross margin and tolerated payback multiply to the number we use? Darpan under-invested in field for a year; Godhuli over-invested for two.

Costing the motion on salary alone. Early sign: CAC that is an executive's cost over closes, with no pre-sales or demand generation. Diagnostic: does every motion's CAC times its new accounts reconcile to total go-to-market spend — at Darpan, ₹391.8 lakh?

Ignoring supply-side cost on a two-sided platform. Early sign: a partnerships team with no revenue target and no cost allocation. Diagnostic: what is the per-account amortised cost of supply bought before demand would pay? Caught late it reads as margin decay.

Letting the channel become the customer. Early sign: a rising share of seats under a falling number of contracts. Diagnostic: what share of paying seats sits with the largest handful of counterparties, and would churn reach us from usage or from them? Gulmohar: a quarter, and from them.

10 · Where experts genuinely disagree

The unit-economics position is that motion is fully determined by the Section 3 identity, the rest being preference dressed as principle. Its evidence: every documented failure, Godhuli included, shows up first as a ratio outside the ceiling. For it to be wrong there must be deals where a motion outside the ceiling still creates value — the lighthouse account whose reference value accrues elsewhere. Proponents answer that this argues for attributing that value, not dropping the rule.

The complexity position holds that price is a proxy and time-to-value the cause: a ₹5 lakh product a customer can configure alone needs no human, and a ₹50,000 product needing a nine-hour integration does. Its evidence is Darpan's reconciliation module and every low-ACV product that grew a support organisation doing sales work. For it to be wrong, complexity would have to be malleable enough that motion is chosen first and the product simplified to fit — as the quote-explainer shows it sometimes is.

The distribution position holds that in intermediated markets motion is not the vendor's choice at all. Its evidence is the Indian POSP market, where licensed sponsorship makes the intermediary the gate and platforms such as Turtlemint and InsuranceDekho run in practice on intermediary distribution. For it to be wrong, a vendor would have to reach and retain agents at scale without sponsor cooperation; Gulmohar's 4,200 direct seats at 71 per cent retention are weak evidence, as consistent with those agents being sponsored anyway.

A quieter fourth split is about horizon: Gulmohar's channel is where payback and lifetime value rank the options oppositely, and that turns on the cost of capital, not the facts.

11 · What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this compares CAC-to-ACV against a remembered threshold. Someone who has internalised it asks for gross margin and payback tolerance first, derives the threshold, then works on the denominator: what ACV was on the last six deals, published or negotiated, who may discount it. They insist on the self-serve counterfactual before crediting a rep, and treat cycle length as float, concentration as a covenant, and a motion as a hiring decision.

12 · What each of them decided

Snigdha Sarangi recommended funding three of the six field executives: the 55.5 per cent ceiling leaves room, but capacity at five deals per executive a year does not yet exist in the pipeline, and reversibility argues for tranches. She took inside sales to five on Exhibit 2's ₹3.11 of gross profit per incremental rupee, and made trailing-six-deal ACV a reported metric, any segment whose payback crosses nine months triggering a motion review, not a price review. Nibedita Patnaik added that the ₹89.6 lakh of annual insurer upkeep would also be reported as acquisition cost per account.

Debasis Routray took the harder decision. He kept the agency channel but capped it — no counterparty above eight per cent of paying seats, a contractual usage feed so churn is visible before it is announced, list pricing on the first hundred seats of any block — and killed the inside-sales pilot. Arupa Sahoo's LTV-to-CAC comparison became the metric the channel is managed on. Both agree the cap will cost growth this year, and neither can prove it is right.

Seeding and Selling Asana

Go-to-Market & Launch — the anatomy of a product that qualifies its own buyers, and the conditions under which that architecture quietly stops working

1. Two desks, ten days apart

On the morning of 3 March 2026, Devika Sundaram opened a spreadsheet she had been avoiding. She is head of growth at Prajwal Labs, a Pune company whose product is a shared workspace for marking up documents — contracts, term sheets, financial models — so that four people in three cities argue in the margins instead of over email. The free tier allows unlimited documents and up to twelve collaborators per workspace. It has worked: 61,000 live free workspaces, 340 paying accounts, ₹31 crore of annual recurring revenue. The board had just asked her to justify employing four account executives rather than sixteen.

The spreadsheet held one account. A non-banking finance company in Mumbai, 4,200 employees, had 470 people using Prajwal across nineteen separate free workspaces — credit, legal, treasury, three regional collections teams. None had paid anything; none, as far as Devika could establish, knew about the other eighteen. Her champion, a deputy manager in credit operations, was enthusiastic, well-liked and had no budget authority whatsoever. Meanwhile a Bengaluru competitor had hired two enterprise reps in January and was, according to a recruiter, calling exactly this kind of account. Devika had to decide whether to reach out this week, on the strength of usage her champion could not authorise her to cite, or wait for the information-security review that nineteen ungoverned workspaces would eventually trigger on their own.

Ten days later and 560 kilometres south, Ramanathan Subbiah was preparing for a board call he expected to lose. He is chief product officer of Agnija Health Systems, a Hyderabad company selling clinical documentation and ward-round software to hospital chains: ₹1.9 crore per contract over three years, a fourteen-month cycle, a signature requiring a chief information officer, a medical superintendent and usually a procurement committee. A new board member who had made money in horizontal SaaS wanted Agnija to "run the Asana playbook" — a free tier for individual doctors, with adoption pulling contracts in behind it.

Ram's objection was not temperamental. A resident cannot lawfully enter patient records into an application the hospital has not approved; under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act the hospital is the data fiduciary and carries the liability, so a free clinical tier would be selling his customers a compliance incident. But his head of design, in London, had made an observation that would not leave him alone: one surface — a drafting assistant that turns a clinician's shorthand into a discharge summary, with no identifiers attached — was already in use on personal phones at four hospitals Agnija had never sold to. Ram had to decide whether that surface was a seed or a distraction.

2. The idea, precisely stated, and who refuses to sign it

Product-led sales is a go-to-market architecture in which qualification is performed by the product rather than a seller. In a sales-led motion a human picks targets from external attributes — headcount, industry, funding — and tries to create belief inside them. In a product-led motion the product is distributed free, spreads through ordinary work, and produces inside the prospect observable behaviour on which a seller then acts. The unit of qualification is the account, not the person: a product-qualified account, or PQA, is an organisation whose aggregate usage has crossed a threshold predicting willingness to contract. Its smaller cousin, the product-qualified lead, is one user's behaviour; confusing the two is the commonest error in the discipline.

The ancestry is long: shareware in the 1980s already understood try-before-you-buy. By the late 2000s products designed for individuals — Skype, Dropbox, later Zoom — arrived inside enterprises through the employee rather than the purchasing department, and Atlassian had built a large software business with famously little field sales, proving the seller was not logically necessary. Asana, founded in 2008 by Dustin Moskovitz and Justin Rosenstein and opened publicly in November 2011, made the invite mechanic structural: assigning work to a colleague who was not yet a user created the invitation as a by-product of the work. OpenView named the pattern product-led growth around 2016; Asana, Slack and Figma then added what pure self-serve lacked — a thin human layer converting sprawling free usage into consolidated, governed contracts.

The problem it solves is economic. Enterprise field sales grew more expensive faster than software grew more valuable; a motion requiring a seller to create belief before any value is delivered carries an acquisition cost only large contracts amortise. Meanwhile the buyer-user split inverted: a browser, a work email and a company card let an employee acquire software without asking anyone. Product-led sales answers both at once — it moves the expensive human to the end, where evidence already exists, and lets the cheap part of the funnel run without payroll.

Three schools disagree substantively about how much of the human to keep.

The distribution school, exemplified by Atlassian's historical model, holds that every rupee spent on a seller is a rupee not spent on making the product spread. It signs that sales is a tax on distribution which documentation, transparent pricing and self-serve procurement largely replace, and refuses to sign that a large enterprise contract inherently requires a human relationship.

The overlay school — Asana's practical position and today's mainstream — holds that the product should do all qualification and none of the closing. It signs that a seller adds value once evidence exists — consolidating shadow accounts, negotiating security and procurement terms, expanding beyond the beachhead — and refuses to sign that free usage converts itself at the enterprise tier, pointing to the fifteen-seat workspace multiplied forty times inside one company: zero revenue, considerable risk.

The sales-primacy school — most clinical, industrial and financial-infrastructure software, and Ram's default — holds that the buyer is an institution with a committee, a budget cycle and a liability, and that individual adoption is at best irrelevant and at worst a governance violation. It signs that category and budget creation require a seller, because no usage creates a line item, and refuses to sign that usage substitutes for a business case.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Expert practice has four stages; the middle two are usually left implicit.

Identity resolution

Nothing works until scattered free usage collapses into organisations. Prajwal's 61,000 workspaces resolve badly: 38 per cent of sign-ups use free-mail addresses and are unattributable; the remaining 9,400 corporate domains collapse to roughly 6,100 legal entities once subsidiaries, regional domains and acquisitions are merged. That merge is data engineering, not growth marketing; teams that skip it discover their largest account only when its security officer calls to ask who authorised nineteen workspaces. Resolution also fixes the denominator of every later metric, which is why threshold arguments are so often entity-resolution arguments in disguise.

Scoring

A seat-count threshold is crude: a dormant account of 400 and a thriving one of 180 are different objects. Prajwal's scoring function, typical of the genre, is a capped weighted composite:

score = 40 · min(1, seats/250) + 30 · (weekly-active ÷ seats) + 20 · min(1, teams/8) + 10 · min(1, 30-day growth ÷ 0.25)

At first detection in September 2025 — 90 seats, 74 per cent weekly-active, 3 teams, 31 per cent monthly growth — the Mumbai account scores 14.4 + 22.2 + 7.5 + 10.0 = 54.1. By March 2026 — 310 seats, 61 per cent active, 11 teams, 18 per cent growth — it is 40.0 + 18.3 + 20.0 + 7.2 = 85.5, against a threshold of 75. The weights are not physics; each is a bet about which behaviour predicts payment. The breadth term is the most informative and the least used, because an account spread across eleven teams has a consolidation problem whether or not the vendor raises it.

Timing

The genuinely quantitative part is the choice of when. Treat expected value at time t as the contract available times the probability of winning it:

EV(t) = S(t) · p · q(t) · (1 − H(t))

S(t) is domain-matched seats, p annual price per seat, q(t) the probability the account says yes given available evidence, and H(t) the hazard that something else has closed the window — a competitor's contract, a security shutdown, a procurement freeze. Evidence rises with time; so does hazard. The product of a rising and a falling factor has an interior maximum, and that maximum answers the timing question.

Capacity and routing

The threshold is not a qualification rule; it is a triage device subordinate to capacity, and treating it otherwise costs money. At a threshold of 75, Prajwal has 140 qualifying accounts. Four account executives can work about eighteen accounts a quarter properly, so capacity is 72. Raising the threshold to 85 to "improve quality" yields 48 accounts at 52 per cent conversion — 25 wins — and leaves 24 rep-slots for cold outbound converting at 6 per cent. Holding it at 75, ranking by score and working the top 72 yields about 41 per cent and roughly 30 wins. Ranking beats gating whenever capacity binds, and capacity almost always binds. The handoff then follows a strict form: the opening message reports usage the customer generated, the champion is credited and co-present rather than bypassed, and what is offered is governance — single sign-on, audit logs, one invoice, deprovisioning — not features the free users already have.

Two second-order effects follow and are routinely missed. Instrumenting for PQAs changes what the product team builds, because the score becomes a roadmap: features raising breadth get funded, features deepening single-team value do not. And once reps are paid on PQAs they learn to manufacture them, coaching friendly champions to open workspaces before quarter end. Both are Goodhart effects, visible as a signal that improves while revenue does not.

4. When the architecture applies, and when it misleads

The idea becomes actively misleading in four situations. Where purchase is high-consideration and low-frequency — a hospital information system, a core banking platform — individual enthusiasm says nothing about institutional intent. Where the free tier has real marginal cost, seeding is a gross-margin decision in a go-to-market costume. Where procurement is mandated, as in public purchases routed through the GeM portal, usage cannot shorten the process and may disqualify the vendor for prior unauthorised deployment. And where the champion's interests diverge from the buyer's — shadow IT the security function must punish — high usage measures institutional anger, not demand.

6. Eight nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

A qualified account is a claim about an organisation; enthusiasm is not evidence. The tell is a champion who cannot name the cost centre that would pay. The obvious reading — the loudest user is the way in — is wrong because that user has the least to lose from a failed evaluation, and colleagues read the advocacy as exactly that.

The free ceiling is a policy instrument with an elasticity, not a price point. The tell is growth and sales arguing about the cap with no shared model of what it does. Raising Prajwal's cap from twelve to twenty lifts the invitation coefficient and delays revenue; cutting it to eight pulls revenue forward and kills the spread that produced the pipeline. The obvious reading — a tighter cap raises conversion — is right for two quarters and wrong for eight.

Activity is not dependency. The tell is usage concentrated in one workflow inside one team, however intense. The diagnostic is the week-eight retained cohort, not the twenty-eight-day active count: what a contract prices is whether people would notice the product vanishing, and only survival curves measure that.

Consolidation is a governance sale wearing a software label. The tell is a winning deck of audit-log and deprovisioning slides with almost no features. The buyer is not purchasing capability, which the organisation already has free, but removal of a risk the free usage itself created.

Latency, not volume, is the scarce resource. The tell is a win rate declining with account age at first contact — easy to compute, almost never computed. The obvious reading of a large free base is stored value; the hazard function says perishable inventory, invisible because lost accounts do not announce themselves.

The free tier is a channel with a cost, and belongs in the same budget as paid media. The tell is that nobody can state the cost of one free workspace for a year. Prajwal's figure — ₹410 a workspace, ₹2.5 crore across the base — proved smaller than its content marketing budget and far more productive: an argument that could not be made until it was costed.

Bottom-up adoption creates an internal opponent before it creates a buyer. The tell is that the first person inside the account who knows the exact number of workspaces sits in security, not the business. Experts sell to that opponent first, arriving with the shadow-account list and an offer to close it, which converts the adversary into the sponsor. The obvious reading — avoid security until the champion has support — inverts the real sequence of power.

The first consolidation often shrinks before it grows. The tell is a contract for fewer seats than the free base held, because deduplication removes forty per cent of accounts and nobody pays for dormant users. Those who have studied the model call this a failed negotiation; those who have run it treat the first contract as the floor of a retention curve and judge the account eighteen months later.
