Stage changes the model more than product type does. Before product-market fit no scoring model is worth building: founders are the sales team, the converted sample is too small to fit anything, and an elaborate rubric only pretends to knowledge. Between the first and second institutional rounds the overlay appears — two to four people, one threshold, manual entity resolution in a spreadsheet — which is the right machinery for that size. At scale it becomes infrastructure and the question shifts to how thresholds, ranking and territories interact with capacity. Late, the tension inverts: a large quota-carrying field organisation experiences the free tier as leakage and lobbies to constrain it, and the company must decide consciously whether it still believes the architecture that built it. What does not change is handoff hygiene — the customer's own data first, the champion credited, governance sold — and treating that as stage-dependent is a common excuse for poor practice.

8. Three worked examples

Shikhavan Analytics, a Gurugram business-intelligence product, had 2,300 free organisations and a seat-based threshold converting at 19 per cent. An analyst noticed the failures were author-only teams — a few heavy builders, nobody else — while the wins were accounts where non-authors consumed dashboards. Shikhavan replaced the seat threshold with "forty or more weekly dashboard views by people who have never built one". Qualifying volume halved to 410; conversion rose to 44 per cent. Wins fell from about 190 to 180, essentially unchanged, but selling cost per win dropped roughly 45 per cent and contracts were larger, because an enterprise licence prices consumption rather than authorship. The correct signal is rarely the obvious one and is found by examining losses.

Panati Systems, a Chennai company turning recorded meetings into decisions and owners, seeded as a pre-AI SaaS product would: unlimited free use for individuals. It reached 40,000 free users in eleven months, each costing ₹62 a month in inference and storage — ₹24.8 lakh a month, ₹2.98 crore a year, against 1.8 per cent conversion. The free tier was not a marketing expense; it was a negative gross margin with a growth chart attached. A meter of ten meetings a month cut cost per free user to ₹19. Sign-ups fell 22 per cent; conversion rose to 4.3 per cent, because the meter created the urgency a seat cap creates in a collaboration product. Free-tier cost fell to ₹68 lakh a year and paid revenue rose. In AI-native products the free tier's shape is set by cost structure first and virality second.

Battiwala Retail Cloud is the failure. The Ahmedabad store-operations company reached 26,000 free workspaces by mid-2024, raised capital on that chart and hired fourteen account executives in one quarter. With no entity resolution and no threshold, the reps did the only thing available: 5,800 workspaces contacted in ninety days, a 2.1 per cent meeting rate, and 41 per cent of those workspaces dormant within sixty days as store managers concluded they were being billed for a free tool. Battiwala added ₹4.6 crore of recurring revenue against ₹9.8 crore of sales cost and damaged the asset the reps had been hired to harvest. Recovery took three quarters and was not analytical. Battiwala cut to five representatives, built domain resolution, set a threshold, and — the part that mattered — stopped contacting free users entirely for two quarters while rebuilding trust, including an explicit promise that the free tier was staying. Eighteen months later it ran ₹21 crore with six representatives. The model was never the hard part; permission was, and permission is re-earned in quarters, not weeks.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether the seller creates value or captures it. The distribution school points to companies reaching very large revenue with negligible field sales, and argues the overlay's measured contribution is confounded: sellers are assigned the accounts most likely to buy, so their win rate is selection, not causation. The overlay school replies that shadow accounts do not consolidate themselves, that security and procurement negotiations need a counterparty, and that the largest contracts in every product-led company were closed by people. One rests on aggregate margin structure, the other on account histories. Randomised assignment to a no-contact arm would settle it; almost nobody runs it, because the revenue foregone is immediate and the knowledge diffuse.

How the free tier should be limited. Seat caps are legible and force the consolidation conversation, but are gamed by parallel workspaces. Feature caps preserve spread and weaken urgency, since a team with what it needs never meets a wall. Usage meters fit AI cost structures and throttle the very power users who generate evidence. All three are held strongly; the answer depends on whether the binding constraint is margin, urgency or spread, which most companies have never determined.

Whether it lowers acquisition cost or relocates it. Sceptics argue the cost moves into engineering and cloud infrastructure, where nobody counts it as acquisition cost, making sales-efficiency comparisons an artefact. Advocates reply that relocated spend is durable: engineering persists, a quarter of outbound calling does not. Both are partly right, and the dispute is about accounting conventions no standard resolves.

Whether PQA models predict anything. Because outcomes are observed only for contacted accounts, virtually every scoring model is fitted on a censored sample and validated against nothing; a model scoring highly the accounts that later convert may merely describe the accounts reps chose to work hard. Those who take this seriously run holdouts — a random tenth of qualified accounts left uncontacted for a quarter — and report lift smaller than the model implies but still positive. For the sceptics to be wrong, uncontacted high-score accounts would have to convert near the contacted rate, which would indict the whole overlay, not just the model.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this argues about thresholds; someone who has internalised it argues about capacity, hazard and permission, and it shows in four behaviours. They compute win rate against account age at first contact and act on the curve even when it says to approach accounts that look too small. They know their free tier's annual cost per workspace and defend it against other channels in the same currency. They treat the prospect's security function as the first customer, not the last obstacle, arriving with the shadow-account list assembled. And they hold the free ceiling as a live, annually revisited decision. Underneath all four is one discipline: never letting a cheap signal stand in for the question of whether an organisation will change its behaviour.

12. What the two protagonists decided

Devika contacted the Mumbai account in March. Her reasoning was the expected-value table: at 310 seats the account was worth ₹18.41 lakh in expectation against ₹15.79 lakh three months later, the decline driven by a hazard she could not influence. She then did three things the number would not have told her to do: asked her champion to co-present rather than going around him; wrote to the information-security head first, listing all nineteen workspaces and offering to close them, so that the first institutional conversation was about control rather than spend; and accepted a fourteen per cent discount for a three-year term, on the view that the first contract was a floor, not a ceiling.

Ram declined the general free tier and kept the enterprise motion, but carved out the drafting surface as a personal-scope product that never touches an identifier, instrumented at hospital-domain level. His argument to the board was that Agnija fails three of five conditions and that a free clinical tier would sell its customers a liability. The carve-out is not a replacement go-to-market but evidence production inside a fourteen-month cycle — the ability to tell a medical superintendent that 60 of her 400 clinicians already use Agnija daily, by choice, before anyone has bought anything. Whether that shortens the cycle or merely decorates it is, on the day he decides, unknown.

  1. Devika's expected-value model treats the hazard rate as exogenous. What could Prajwal Labs do to lower it, and would those actions be cheaper than contacting accounts earlier?
  2. Battiwala's recovery required two quarters of deliberately not selling. Under what board and funding conditions is that decision available, and what would you do if it were not?
  3. If Ram's carve-out succeeds and hospital-domain usage begins to predict wins, at what point should Agnija reorganise around it — and what would it have to give up to do so?

13. Going deeper

Product-led sales (PQA / PQL) states the mechanism formally, separating the scoring problem from the routing problem, which this page treats together. What a GTM strategy is places seed-and-sell inside the choices about segment, channel and pricing that constrain it. Your first 100 users covers the stage before this machinery exists, where seeding is done by hand. Channels: paid, owned, earned gives the currency that makes the free tier arguable as a channel with a cost per acquisition. Inbound vs outbound clarifies what remains for outbound once the product qualifies its own accounts. Product-led growth is the parent architecture, self-serve path included. Sales-led growth is what Ram defends, and why it persists in institutional markets is what stops this playbook being used where it destroys value.

Seeding and Selling Asana

Go-to-Market, Growth & Monetisation — how a free product finds the moment to become a paid one

1. A job that should not have existed

In January 2015, Oliver Jay arrived at Asana's San Francisco office to take on a role that, on paper, made little sense. Asana was already spreading fast and needed almost no one to sell it. Dustin Moskovitz and Justin Rosenstein, the two Facebook alumni who founded the company in 2008 and opened it to the public in November 2011, had built it on a simple premise: let a team start for nothing, and let daily use make the case that a salesperson never could. It had worked almost too well. By the time Jay arrived, employees inside Uber, Spotify and Pinterest were running real work through Asana boards, and none of those companies had ever signed a contract. They did not need to — Asana's free tier covered any workspace of up to fifteen people, and nothing stopped fifty different fifteen-person teams inside one building from each opening its own.

That was the problem on Jay's desk. Somewhere inside dozens of large companies, hundreds of employees depended on Asana every day, invisible to Asana itself because no one had ever added them up into a single account. Do nothing, and a rival's sales team could walk into any of those companies, offer one consolidated contract, and absorb years of quiet, unpaid adoption in a single meeting. Push too hard, too soon, and a clumsy sales call would look like a company charging for something its own champions believed was free — unwinding the very trust that had built the funnel. Jay's task was to decide how, and when, a human being should finally get involved.

2. The idea: let the product sell first

What Jay was hired to build became known as product-led sales, sometimes shortened to "seed and sell," and it sits close to what the venture firm OpenView Partners, from around 2016, popularised as product-led growth. The idea is simple to state: instead of a salesperson introducing a product to a prospect, the product introduces itself for free, spreads through ordinary use, and generates its own evidence of value; a human joins only once that evidence has accumulated inside an organisation that can actually pay. The unit that matters is not one enthusiastic user — a "product-qualified lead," or PQL, in the vocabulary that grew up around this idea — but the account: a whole company or business unit whose combined usage crosses a threshold worth calling a "product-qualified account," or PQA.

Product-led sales solves a specific mismatch. Traditional sales-led go-to-market assumes a company can identify, in advance, who might want its product and knock on that door. Bottom-up, self-serve products break that assumption entirely: the product is already inside the building before anyone in sales even knows the company exists. The sentence Jay could repeat in any meeting without sounding glib was this: let the product do the selling until the data says a human should follow up — never before.

3. How it actually works

Turning that sentence into a working system took several distinct pieces of machinery, and the middle three are the ones most people leave implicit. Entry had to be frictionless: anyone could open an account with a work email in under a minute, no salesperson in sight. The product needed a built-in reason for one user to recruit the next — assigning a task to a colleague who was not yet on Asana automatically invited them, so the invite chain was a side effect of ordinary work, not a marketing campaign. And the free ceiling itself, fifteen people per workspace, let the product spread widely long before it needed to spread expensively.

The steps usually left unspoken come next. Someone has to notice, computationally, that forty separate fifteen-person free workspaces registered with the same "@uber.com" domain are, in fact, one very large account with zero visibility to Asana's own systems — without that domain-matching, the seed-and-sell motion has no eyes. Someone has to define what "ready" means: not raw headcount alone, but headcount combined with how many of those users are still active week to week, since a large but dormant account is a different signal from a smaller, thriving one. And someone has to route the qualified account to a person whose opening message cites usage the company has already generated — "your marketing group alone opened forty projects last quarter" — rather than a pitch built from nothing. What follows is a conversion, not a cold sale: many ungoverned free workspaces become one paid, centrally administered plan with single sign-on and a named account owner, from which further expansion continues.

4. A worked example: Tatini Freight

Consider a stylised account. Tatini Freight is a 3,000-employee logistics company headquartered in Pune whose operations staff quietly started using Asana's free tier in January 2016, one small team at a time, with no one in IT or finance aware it was happening.

Asana's account team reaches out in November 2016, citing the nine workspaces rather than pitching cold. At the Business-plan list price of the day, roughly $24.99 per user per month, formalising all 260 seats into one contract comes to 260 × $24.99 × 12 ≈ $77,970 a year — call it about ₹64 lakh at a rough ₹83-to-the-dollar rate. The number is not asserted; it is 260 seats, one price, twelve months, added up.

Now change one input: suppose the account team had waited for a stricter rule — 500 domain-matched users — before reaching out. Growth continues to April 2017, when the account does reach 500 users at 58% weekly-active. But by then a rival vendor's own enterprise sales team has already approached Tatini Freight's IT department directly and signed 350 of those seats onto a competing platform, leaving Asana only 150 to formalise: 150 × $24.99 × 12 ≈ $44,982, about ₹37 lakh — roughly $33,000, or ₹27 lakh, less than converting at the 260-seat mark, plus 350 people's daily habit now built around someone else's product. Nothing about the price or the product changed. Only the number of months Asana waited before saying hello did.

5. Nuances a learner must hold onto

A product-qualified account is not a product-qualified lead

One employee enthusing about Asana in a Slack channel is a PQL — one person's behaviour. A product-qualified account is a claim about an organisation: that enough of its people, across enough of its structure, now depend on the tool for a contract conversation to make sense. Pitching the loudest champion, who is very often not the budget holder, is a common way to lose weeks on a deal that was never theirs to sign.

The free ceiling is a lever, not a law

Fifteen free seats per workspace was a dial Asana chose to set, not a constant it discovered. Turning it up buys more spread at the cost of delayed revenue; turning it down converts revenue sooner while choking off the very virality that built accounts like Tatini Freight. Every setting trades one goal against the other — none solves both.

Usage growth correlates with willingness to pay; it does not guarantee it

An account can run 260 free users for years for the simple reason that free is good enough, with no urgency behind it. And once a fifteen-person ceiling starts to bind, some teams do not come to sales at all — they quietly open an eleventh and twelfth free workspace to dodge it, which is exactly why the counting has to come from domain-matching, not from what any one team reports about itself.

It applies where adoption can start before approval does

Horizontal, high-frequency tools with a low per-seat cost and a built-in invite mechanic — task boards, chat, file sharing — spread the way Asana did. A hospital's radiology imaging system, evaluated once and bought by a single budget owner, has no equivalent bottom-up path; there is no free trial a radiologist quietly spreads to fifty colleagues.

What usage data cannot tell you

Instrumentation shows that 260 people open the product five days a week. It cannot show who controls the software budget, when a rival's contract comes up for renewal, or whether procurement will insist on a formal tender regardless of how much people already like the tool. A product-led signal answers "is anyone using this," not "who can sign for it," and skipping the second question is how good pipeline turns into a stalled deal.

It is easily confused with growth hacking

A pile of sign-ups from a discount code or a referral contest can look, on a raw dashboard, exactly like organic spread — both show up as a spike in new accounts. They are not the same signal. A coupon-driven sign-up says people responded to an incentive; a sustained, domain-matched account says the product already earns its keep without one. Selling against the first is selling on hope.

Timing cuts both ways

Reach out while usage is still shallow, and the call reads as a sales team interrupting a free tool people currently enjoy — the very goodwill the strategy exists to protect. Wait too long, and either a rival's sales team reaches the account's IT department first, as very nearly happened at Tatini Freight, or the company's own security function notices hundreds of ungoverned accounts and shuts the whole thing down rather than risk it. The window closes from both ends.

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and early versus at scale

In a consumer product such as a music-streaming app, seeding is entirely individual and "sales" barely exists: the person using the free tier is also the one who decides whether to upgrade, so a self-serve prompt at the moment of friction does the whole job. Asana's world is different precisely because the user and the buyer are different people — an individual employee adopts it, but a finance or IT leader eventually has to sign for it — which is exactly why an account-level signal like the PQA, and a human to act on it, earn their keep. In a two-sided marketplace, seeding has to happen on both sides at once, and the "sell" step often lands on the supply side: a food-delivery platform, say, seeds restaurants with free listing tools and only later sells them paid promotion, once enough demand-side pull already justifies the ask.

Stage matters as much as product type. In an early-stage company, seeding is the entire go-to-market function; the founders are the sales team, and there is rarely enough data yet to know which usage patterns predict revenue, so building an elaborate scoring model too soon is itself a mistake. At scale, the seed function becomes durable infrastructure — domain-matching, a PQA-scoring model, a dedicated account team — and the open question shifts from whether product-led sales works at all to which threshold and routing rules protect champions while still catching the account before a rival does.

7. Common mistakes

8. What good looks like

Picture the same decision handled well. An account team notices Tatini Freight crossing the 200-user, 50%-active rule in November 2016 and waits one more week to see the pattern hold before acting. The first message an operations director receives does not ask her to buy anything; it notes, correctly, that nine of her teams already coordinate freight schedules in Asana and offers to fold them into one plan with single sign-on and one bill, at no disruption to how anyone already works. The champions inside those nine teams are credited internally rather than bypassed. The contract that results looks less like a sale and more like a company finally getting official credit — and proper security controls — for something it had already decided to depend on. Renewal, the following year, is not really a negotiation.

9. What Jay decided

Jay's team built a small overlay group rather than a conventional sales floor: a handful of people whose job was to watch domain-matched usage, apply the threshold rule, and open every conversation with data the customer had already generated. He resisted the two easy failure modes on either side of that decision — hiring a large outbound sales force that would have cold-called Asana's own happiest free users, and doing nothing while competitors' sales teams picked off the largest ungoverned accounts one by one. The reasoning was that the free product had already done the hardest part of selling, which is proving the thing works; the remaining job was narrow and specific — find the accounts where that proof was strongest, and make paying for it easier than not paying for it.

What to learn next, and why: net revenue retention, the metric that tracks whether accounts like Tatini Freight keep expanding after the first contract, because seeding and selling once is only half the model — the other half is whether the same account grows for years afterward.

Two questions worth sitting with: Where in your own product might organic usage already be creating an account no one has ever aggregated? And if you started charging for what is free today, would the product still spread — or has the free tier already been the thing quietly earning you every customer you now have?

Inbound vs Outbound: Direction, Intent and the Arithmetic of Being Found

Rarely a question about channels; almost always about whether the demand already exists.

1. Two rooms, three weeks apart

On 11 February 2026, in a glass-walled room off Bannerghatta Road in Bengaluru, Ira Chaturvedi presented a chart she could not make look better. Ira ran growth at Potaka AI, which sold evaluation and observability infrastructure to teams building on large language models: ₹31 crore of recurring revenue, 2,900 self-serve accounts at ₹2,400 a seat per month, 210 team accounts at a median ₹18 lakh a year, four enterprise contracts above ₹1 crore. It had raised ₹64 crore eighteen months earlier, largely on one asset: 240 technical articles that in mid-2025 pulled 190,000 organic sessions a month and 1,900 sign-ups.

By January 2026 sessions had fallen to 118,000 and sign-ups to 1,240. Impressions were flat; clicks were not. Developers had stopped clicking through because their coding assistants answered the question directly, occasionally citing Potaka, usually not: the pull engine was being read by machines rather than buyers. Ira's board wanted eight sales development representatives and four account executives — ₹3.2 crore a year against nineteen months of runway — to find the roughly 3,400 engineering organisations worldwide building enough on LLMs to need what Potaka sold.

Three weeks later, on 3 March, Girish Mattoo sat before a whiteboard in Pune listing 31 distributors. Girish was chief commercial officer of Samudra Instruments, maker of a point-of-care haematology analyser — a ₹6.8 lakh CDSCO-licensed device with a ₹96,000-a-year cloud subscription — sold to laboratories and small hospitals through distributors in fourteen states, plus nine direct engineers for the large lab chains. Its new product, an AI-assisted slide pre-screening module, was software only, ₹1.4 lakh a year, and ran on competitors' analysers too. It could in principle be sold to any of India's 48,000 pathology labs with no distributor and no purchase order.

Girish had ₹4.6 crore. One faction wanted twelve more field engineers; another wanted content aimed at pathologists — NABL accreditation, turnaround times, slide-review quality — on the theory that pathologists, unlike lab owners, do search. Neither had noticed that Girish's question was not Ira's, despite the identical words.

2. The idea, and the four schools that disagree about it

Inbound is a motion in which the buyer initiates: they have a question, they look for an answer, and the seller is findable at the point of looking. Outbound is a motion in which the seller initiates: they select a buyer, construct a reason for the timing, and interrupt. The distinguishing variable is not the medium — an email, a call or an event can carry either — but who moves first, and therefore whether the seller captures intent that already exists or manufactures intent that does not.

The practice is older than the vocabulary. Measured direct marketing dates to Lester Wunderman in the 1960s; outbound's intellectual content — build a list, test a message, count the replies — was settled long before software. The modern pairing of the terms belongs to Brian Halligan and Dharmesh Shah, who founded HubSpot in 2006 on the claim that buyers could now research independently and would punish interruption. Seth Godin's Permission Marketing (1999) supplied the moral argument; the search engine supplied the mechanism.

What is forgotten is that outbound's most rigorous formulation appeared at the height of inbound's ascendancy. Aaron Ross's Predictable Revenue (2011) industrialised outbound by splitting the seller's role into prospecting and closing and treating pipeline as a manufacturable quantity. The same year, Dixon and Adamson's The Challenger Sale argued that the best sellers do not answer the buyer's question but reframe it. Together these rebut the pull thesis: if the buyer's framing is wrong, being findable by their search is being findable for the wrong thing.

Four positions are live, and an expert can state what each will and will not sign.

Figure 1. The schools differ less over channels than over two prior questions: whether the demand is already in the market, and whether measurement can locate it.

The pull school will sign: buyers who can self-educate prefer to, and a seller absent from that education is disqualified before contact. It will not sign that content creates demand in a category the buyer cannot name. The outbound industrialists will sign: for enumerable, high-value populations pipeline is a production process with a capacity equation, and waiting to be found forfeits control of timing. They will not sign that volume substitutes for targeting. The availability school — Ehrenberg-Bass, and Binet and Field's 60:40 split — will sign that perhaps 5% of a category's buyers are in market at any moment, so both motions are activation tactics fighting over a thin slice while the other 95% are won by memory built years earlier. It will not sign that this year's pipeline can come from brand spend alone. The dark-social school will sign that "inbound" is often an artefact of last-touch attribution: the buyer heard a podcast, asked a colleague, then typed the company's name into a search box, and the CRM recorded organic search. It will not sign that measurement is hopeless, only that the instrument must be a free-text source field.

3. Mechanics: three pieces of arithmetic experts actually run

Competent practitioners compare average cost per acquired customer. Experts run three other calculations first, and each changes the answer.

3a. The intent ceiling

Inbound cannot produce more customers than there is existing intent to capture, and that quantity is measurable. Ira's team assembled 340 search terms a buyer of evaluation tooling might use and totalled their volume at 210,000 searches a month worldwide. A realistic click-share ceiling for a non-incumbent ranking in the top three for most of them is 28%, or 58,800 sessions; at Potaka's 1.1% sign-up rate, 647 sign-ups a month against the 1,240 Potaka already had. The engine was not underperforming — it was past the ceiling of the pool it could address, and each marginal article bought cheaper traffic of lower relevance. The 38% click decline against flat impressions said worse: the ceiling itself was falling.

3b. Marginal, not average, cost per customer

The equimarginal principle says a budget is optimally allocated when the last rupee spent on each activity buys the same output. The question is therefore not which motion has lower CAC but which has lower CAC on the next tranche. Ira built the following, in ₹50 lakh tranches per quarter.

Table 1. Inbound's marginal cost rises as the intent pool empties. Outbound's falls before it rises: the first tranche buys a manager, a data subscription and a playbook the next two reuse.

The shape of the outbound column is the point. Inbound is concave: the best keywords go first and every later one is worse. Outbound is S-shaped, because the fixed costs of a working motion — list infrastructure, a manager who listens to calls, a message through four revisions — are paid before the first incremental deal and amortised across the rest. Hence a consequence teams learn expensively: you cannot test outbound small. A single SDR samples the worst part of the curve, and a bad result there says almost nothing about the motion at scale. Inbound can be tested small honestly, because its first tranche is its best.

3c. The time constant, discounted

The third calculation is the one boards decide on. Inbound has a lag — nothing bookable for roughly eleven months, then compounding as the asset base grows. Outbound ramps in three to six months, then delivers flat headcount-linear output with no compounding. Two second-order effects sit underneath and both are mis-booked. First, outbound produces inbound: when Potaka later ran an eight-week campaign into 1,100 named accounts, branded search rose 23% and fourteen of the thirty-one "organic" demo requests that quarter came from domains on the outbound list, the CRM crediting inbound for demand outbound created. Second, terminal value: content keeps producing after spend stops, while a disbanded SDR team produces nothing. Neither appears in a cost-per-lead table.

4. Conditions, stated as testable claims

The choice can be reduced to five claims that are true or false about a specific business, each checkable before spending.

The idea becomes actively misleading in three situations. First, a genuinely new category, where C4 is false: there is no search volume for a problem nobody has named, so an inbound plan measures itself against a denominator of zero and concludes, wrongly, that there is no market. Second, a procurement-mediated purchase — government tenders, hospital chains buying capital equipment, public-sector banks — where the buyer cannot act on information outside a process content never enters. Samudra's nine direct engineers exist because a ₹6.8 lakh capital item in a NABL-accredited lab goes through a technical specification, and the firm that helps write it wins. Third, an intermediated market, where the person who searches, the person who decides and the person who pays are three people, and the inbound lead is reliably the least powerful.

5. Hard edge cases, and what mature companies really do

Multi-product. Samudra's situation is the common one: a capital product sold outbound through distributors, and a software product whose economics demand self-serve. The seam is organisational: the module cannot be sold inbound into a territory a distributor holds a contractual claim on, so channel conflict masquerades as a motion debate. Mature firms quietly pay the distributor a reduced margin on inbound-originated revenue in their territory, which is cheaper than the alternative and never described that way in the strategy deck.

Two-sided. The two sides of a marketplace usually need opposite motions, and running one across both is a standard early failure: the scarce side must be pushed, the abundant side pulls itself. Bandargah Exchange, matching pharmaceutical brands with contract manufacturers, called each of 1,400 licensed formulation units individually, because a factory with idle capacity does not search for a marketplace — it calls the two brokers it knows. Brands arrived by searching "third-party manufacturing Baddi." A blended CAC would have hidden that one side cost sixty times the other and was worth it.

Regulated. Where claims are regulated, inbound has a ceiling on usefulness. Samudra cannot publish comparative accuracy content without clinical evidence and CDSCO-consistent labelling, as a fund cannot publish returns outside SEBI's disclosure rules. Regulated inbound drifts toward generic education that ranks but does not differentiate; expert practice accepts that it buys credibility rather than leads, and budgets it as such.

AI-native. Two things are happening at once, in opposite directions. Answer engines are compressing inbound's click-through, shifting the objective from ranking to being the source a model cites — a craft favouring structured primary material over volume. Meanwhile generative tooling has driven the cost of a personalised cold email to near zero and flooded inboxes: B2B reply rates have fallen from roughly 4% a decade ago to well under 1%, while 2024 bulk-sender authentication rules and India's DPDP Act consent regime raised the cost of being delivered at all. Both motions got harder in the same eighteen months, for unrelated reasons.

At the organisational seam. The deepest failures are structural. SDRs reporting to marketing optimise meetings booked; under sales, meetings held. Marketing is paid on lead volume and sales on closed revenue, so the definition of a qualified lead becomes a negotiated political object rather than a measurement. Mature companies handle this less elegantly than they claim: one pipeline-generation number owned by one executive, the split no longer reported to the board, and the distinction alive only inside the planning model.

6. Eight distinctions between the expert and the competent

The ceiling is intent, not effort. The competent practitioner answers flat inbound growth by publishing more; the expert computes the intent pool first and sees that beyond it content buys traffic of falling relevance. Tell-tale sign: sessions rising while sign-ups per session fall, and the keyword list widening into topics the product does not serve. The content is not weak. The market for that question is finished.

Outbound's real product is category education, delivered late. Sixty to ninety days after a campaign branded search rises, and the competent practitioner reads that as inbound improving. The expert instruments it, because outbound's measured return is understated and its true payback shorter than the CRM shows. Tell-tale sign: branded search tracking SDR activity lagged a quarter, nothing else changing.

Attribution is a biased instrument and the fix is a text box. Last-touch credits whatever sits closest to purchase, nearly always search. The expert runs a mandatory free-text source field and reconciles it against the CRM quarterly. Tell-tale sign: the CRM says organic search is 60% of pipeline while the free text says a podcast, a former colleague and one community. Customers are not misremembering; the tracking parameter cannot see past the last click.

The largest accounts never fill in forms. Inbound selects for buyers small enough to act alone, so contract value correlates inversely with inbound origination. Tell-tale sign: median inbound ACV at half median outbound ACV or less, stable across quarters. Treating that as a lead-quality problem mistakes a structural selection effect for an execution failure.

Low ACV plus outbound fails on payback, not on CAC. Potaka's ₹2,400 seat tier could be sold by a rep at a CAC that looks fine against lifetime value, and still cannot be: the cash returns over four years and the rep is paid monthly. The expert separates unit economics, payback period and sales capacity. Tell-tale sign: a plan that is LTV-positive and starves the company anyway.

In India the pull channel is often not search. Much Indian SMB discovery runs through the chartered accountant, the dealer, the association WhatsApp group and the district trade body — inbound in the strict sense, invisible to analytics, unreachable by search optimisation. The expert asks where the buyer's trusted intermediary sits before asking what the buyer types. Tell-tale sign: strong rankings, real traffic, and a pipeline that does not move.

Content depreciates and carries a maintenance obligation. Rankings erode and facts stale; in technical categories a two-year-old post is a liability. Teams book content as capital expenditure and never fund the refresh, so the library grows while yield per item falls. The expert budgets about a third of capacity to maintenance and measures traffic per live article. Tell-tale sign: article count up 40% year on year, sessions up 8%.

The handoff interval outranks either budget. Response time to an inbound request is the highest-leverage uncontrolled variable in most companies: five minutes against five hours is a large multiple on qualification odds, and closing the gap costs nothing. The expert audits it before debating allocation. Tell-tale sign: a median first-response time nobody can quote.

7. Where the difference by product type is real, and where it is not

In consumer products outbound in the classical sense barely exists: a human touch costs more than lifetime value by an order of magnitude. Nauka Wellness, a sleep app, carried a lifetime value of ₹1,180 against ₹340 per human contact — four touches and the user is unprofitable before subscribing. What consumer companies call outbound is paid advertising, push in spirit but priced per impression; the useful axis is intent-matched versus interruptive.

In B2B the distinction is real and sharpens with contract value: above roughly ₹25 lakh a year the buying committee passes four people, at which point no single inbound lead represents the account and outbound's reach to the economic buyer becomes decisive. Platforms and marketplaces split by side. Hardware adds a third direction the binary omits — through-channel — where dealers hold the relationship and the manufacturer creates pull the channel converts.

For AI products the difference is not yet stable. Where the product is developer-facing, the product itself is the best inbound asset — an open-source component, a public benchmark, a usable free tier — as has been true of developer tools since long before AI. Where an AI application is sold to a business function, the pattern resembles ordinary B2B software with a shorter education curve, because buyers arrive convinced something in the category matters and unsure what. The scarce commodity has moved from convincing a buyer the problem exists to being the specific answer against a budget that already exists.

Stage changes the constraint, not the logic. A seed-stage company has no content history and cannot wait eleven months, so it does outbound or founder-led selling whatever the theory says, and its useful question is which targets teach it most. A growth-stage company has the data to compute Table 1 honestly, and is where marginal analysis pays. A mature company holds search authority a challenger cannot replicate and a channel with contractual claims, so its question is allocation, not choice.

8. Three worked examples

Bandargah Exchange: opposite motions on two sides. In year one Bandargah spent ₹1.9 crore on supply-side outbound — six field executives calling 1,400 contract manufacturers, 312 of which onboarded, a CAC of ₹60,900 each — against ₹41 lakh of content ranking for third-party manufacturing terms, producing 1,870 brand sign-ups at ₹2,200. On blended numbers the supply programme looked indefensible and was nearly cut. But each manufacturer supported a median ₹27 lakh of annual gross merchandise value against ₹3.1 lakh per brand: the expensive side was the valuable one, and blending had hidden it.

Samudra Instruments: pull through a channel. Before the March meeting Samudra ran a test that shaped everything after: nine pieces on inter-laboratory quality control for NABL surveillance audits, promoted through two pathologist associations rather than search, for ₹22 lakh. Directly attributable revenue was zero. But in 38 of 61 demonstrations that quarter the lab had already seen the material, and demonstration-to-order conversion in those 38 ran at 34% against 19% elsewhere — fifteen points on 240 annual demonstrations, roughly ₹2.4 crore of device revenue. Any lead-attribution measurement would have killed it.

Kashti Commerce: good inbound aimed at a buyer who did not search. Between 2022 and 2024 Kashti, selling billing software to retail chains and ambitious standalone stores, built 900 articles on GST filing, stock reconciliation and shrinkage, spent ₹11 crore and reached 320,000 monthly sessions. Content-sourced pipeline ran at 4% of total. The decision-maker turned out to be a store owner who transacted in Marathi and Hindi, did not read English business content, and bought software from the dealer who sold him his billing printer; the traffic was students, competitors' employees and accountants. Recovery inverted the model over three quarters: 1,900 hardware dealers at 22% of first-year subscription, the best forty articles rewritten as dealer-facing WhatsApp collateral, workshops in eleven cities. Dealer-originated revenue reached 27% of new bookings. The content was sound; the theory of how it reached the buyer was not.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

None of these diagnostics needs new infrastructure; each can be answered in a week by someone willing to ask a plain question of a system already running. What prevents it is that the question embarrasses whoever owns the programme, which is why the diagnostics belong to someone whose bonus does not depend on the answer.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Is the intent pool exogenous? The pull school holds that demand exists and the seller's job is to be present at it. The demand-creation camp holds that the pool is itself made by marketing, so a firm capturing only existing search harvests a field someone else planted. The first rests on search volume's stability against any one firm's spend; the second on categories — CRM, marketing automation, observability — whose volume a few firms created by spending heavily on education. The first is wrong if a mid-sized firm can reliably lift category search volume on a bounded budget; the second if categories grow without vendor spend.

Is attribution recoverable? One camp believes a well-specified multi-touch model on clean data allocates credit usefully. The other believes journeys are mostly untracked — conversations, podcasts, private communities — so any model is precision applied to a biased sample, leaving self-reported source and geographic holdouts as the only trustworthy instruments. Its evidence is that the two methods disagree substantially within one dataset; its weakness is that self-report cannot allocate at keyword level. Cheap large-scale holdouts would settle it.

Does brand-building substitute for either motion? The availability school says most category buyers are out of market, so activation fights over a thin slice while memory built earlier decides who is considered. Sceptics reply that the evidence base is packaged goods with short cycles and many buyers, and that extending it to a category of 3,400 accounts is an assumption, not a finding. The sceptics are wrong if unaided awareness lifts activation returns in B2B; the school is wrong if concentrated markets reward targeting over memory.

Has AI changed the answer or only the costs? One view: answer engines are a distribution shift like the move from directories to search, and the winners will again be those producing the primary material machines cite. The other: a structural break, because an intermediary that answers the question has no incentive to pass the reader on, converting inbound from lead generation into brand presence that cannot be measured the old way. Nobody has three years of data; Ira is deciding without it.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this argues about which motion is better and reaches for benchmarks. Someone who has internalised it does four things differently. They size the intent pool and the enumerable account list first, because those two numbers cap each motion before execution is discussed. They think marginally rather than on averages, asking "how much" before "which." They instrument the interaction between the motions — branded search after outbound, demonstration conversion after content — because that is where most of the value and all of the mis-attribution lives. And they hold the vocabulary loosely: where a case does not fit the binary, they describe what is happening rather than force a label. Asked "inbound or outbound," the expert does not answer; they ask what fraction of the buying population is in market this quarter, and whether anyone can name them.

12. What Ira and Girish decided

Ira funded neither proposal as written. She halved content production and redirected that capacity to what the intent-ceiling analysis implied: primary material an answer engine would cite — a public, versioned benchmark of evaluation methods, and an open-source harness that was itself the product's front door — plus a rebuilt free tier, on the reasoning that if the article could no longer be the entry point, the software had to be. She hired three SDRs rather than eight, pointed only at organisations already running the free tier above a usage threshold, converting the list problem into an inspection of her own telemetry. She told the board the plan missed the number by 40%, and that climbing a non-convex cost curve with twelve new people was a larger bet than the runway supported.

Girish refused the framing. He kept the twelve field engineers off the budget and split ₹4.6 crore three ways: a pathologist-facing content and association programme measured on demonstration-conversion rather than leads; a distributor enablement layer putting the same material in dealers' hands with 22% margin on attached software; and a small direct team for the 240 lab chains whose purchases run through a technical specification. The module would be sold self-serve only in the nine states with no exclusive distributor — a compromise with a contract rather than a strategy.

  1. Ira's decision rests on the claim that Potaka's telemetry is a better targeting list than any purchased database. What would have to be true of free-tier adoption for that claim to fail, and how would she know within one quarter?
  2. Samudra measured content on demonstration-conversion rather than leads. What does a company give up when it adopts a metric no attribution system can independently verify, and when is that trade worth making?
  3. Kashti's content was well made and aimed at the wrong reader. At what point in two years was the failure first detectable, and which single question, asked earlier, would have surfaced it?

13. Going deeper

Channels: paid, owned, earned
The orthogonal classification: direction and ownership are independent axes, which is what lets you see paid search as bought access to inbound intent.
What a GTM strategy is
The container this sits in: segment, value proposition, motion and pricing must agree, or the other three will overturn the motion.
Your first 100 users

Product-led growth
The strongest form of inbound, where the product rather than the content is the discovery asset — Ira's pivot.
Sales-led growth
What committing to outbound implies: quota design, ramp, segmentation and the capacity equation that caps growth.
Product-led sales (PQA/PQL)

Inbound vs Outbound: Pull with Content or Push with Outreach?

1. A board slide with fourteen months on it

On the second Monday of March 2025, Devika Nair, head of growth at Tantuka Systems, stared at one line in a board deck: fourteen months of runway. Tantuka sold workflow software that let mid-sized manufacturers — apparel exporters in Tiruppur, auto-component makers in Pune — track a purchase order from raw material to shipped container without four spreadsheets and a WhatsApp group. The company had forty-three paying customers, roughly eighteen crore rupees in annual recurring revenue, and a board mandate to reach forty crore by March 2026: sixty new accounts at an average contract value of thirty-seven lakh rupees, sold to a fifty-two-year-old operations head who had never heard of Tantuka and did not read product blogs.

Devika had two proposals and a budget for exactly one. Her content lead wanted to double down on what was already working in a small way: search-optimised guides on export documentation, a monthly webinar with a customs consultant, a free purchase-order template that had quietly become the company's best-performing page. Give it nine more months, the argument went, and organic demo requests would compound. Her newly hired sales director wanted six outbound account executives armed with a list of eleven hundred named manufacturers, cold-calling and cold-emailing procurement heads directly. Both proposals were reasonable; both could not be funded at once. The decision was really about whether Tantuka would pull its next sixty customers toward itself, or push its way into their calendars — and which made sense with fourteen months to prove it could grow.

2. The idea, defined precisely

Inbound go-to-market means creating something of value — information, a tool, a reputation — that causes a prospective buyer to seek the seller out on their own initiative, once the buyer already has the problem in mind. Outbound go-to-market means the seller initiates contact with a buyer who was not, at that moment, looking — cold email, cold calls, or a salesperson at a trade stall. The distinction is not the channel; email can carry either motion, and so can a phone call. It is about who moves first: in inbound, the buyer's own search is the trigger; in outbound, the seller manufactures one.

The vocabulary is younger than the practice — salespeople have always cold-called, and word of mouth has always pulled customers in — but the terms were popularised together around 2005 by Brian Halligan and Dharmesh Shah, the founders of HubSpot, as a contrast to what they called "interruption marketing": trade-show booths, purchased mailing lists, banner ads buyers had grown skilled at ignoring. Their claim was that as buyers gained the ability to research on their own, sellers findable at the moment of search would out-compete sellers still shouting into a market that had learned to tune shouting out. That claim was correct for a specific kind of buyer and badly incomplete for others — exactly what Devika needed to work out before Friday.

The sentence Devika could say in the boardroom without sounding glib was this: inbound earns attention by solving a problem the buyer already knows they have; outbound creates attention for a problem the buyer has not yet framed as urgent — and which one wins depends on whether our buyer is searching yet.

3. The mechanics, step by step

Inbound has a mechanism, not just a mood, and skipping its steps is where teams go wrong. Step one: identify a question the buyer already types or asks a peer — for Tantuka's operations head, "how to avoid customs delays on export shipments," not "workflow software." Step two: produce content that answers it completely enough to stand alone; content written to bait a lead rather than answer a question gets abandoned mid-page and never ranks. Step three: distribute — search optimisation, citation by others, presence in communities the buyer frequents, such as an exporters' association forum. Step four, often left implicit, is capture and nurture: a reader is not a lead, and converting one into a named contact requires an offer worth an email address, then a sequence that keeps delivering value until they are ready for sales. Step five is the handoff — deciding when a reader has shown enough intent to be worth a salesperson's time.

Outbound runs the opposite direction. Step one: build a list, an ideal customer profile precise enough to filter a database down to real prospects, not just any manufacturer. Step two: find a trigger that makes an unsolicited message feel timely rather than random — funding raised, a plant opened — since outreach with no trigger reads as spam and earns a sub-1% reply rate. Step three: write a message specific to the recipient's likely situation rather than generic about the product. Step four, often skipped, is cadence: most replies come from the fourth or fifth touch, so one cold email tests one email, not outbound itself. Step five is qualification on the call — budget, authority, need, timeline — before investing further selling time. Both motions, done properly, are expensive and skill-dependent; the myth that inbound is "free" and outbound is "just effort" is what the next section dismantles.

Figure 1. Inbound and outbound are mirror-image processes: one is discovered, the other is initiated. Neither skips a step without a cost showing up later.

4. The arithmetic Devika actually ran

Devika built two models, both for a single quarter. Inbound: the PO-template page pulled nine thousand monthly visitors, of whom 2.1% (189) downloaded a gated compliance checklist, of whom 12% (23) booked a demo, of whom 30% closed — 7 customers at an average contract value of ₹31 lakh, since inbound tended to land smaller first-time buyers. The content function cost ₹9 lakh a month, ₹27 lakh a quarter: seven customers against that spend gives a blended acquisition cost near ₹3.9 lakh, assuming the prior two quarters' conversion rates hold — which they might not, since a chunk of that traffic came from one guide ranking for one keyword a competitor could also target.

Outbound: six account executives at ₹4.5 lakh per month each (₹27 lakh a quarter), each making 40 qualified conversations a month against the list, converting 8% at an average contract value of ₹42 lakh — reps targeted larger accounts, since the cost per touch justified aiming higher. At full productivity that is 58 customers, but new hires never ramp immediately; a quarter-one output at 40% of steady state gives roughly 23, an implied CAC near ₹1.17 lakh once revenue is counted, though the cash cost per logo, ignoring the ramp discount, is closer to ₹7 lakh.

Devika then changed one input: what if average contract value fell to ₹28 lakh, because reps under quota pressure discounted to close faster? Revenue fell from roughly ₹9.7 crore to ₹6.4 crore, and because the whole case rested on accounts large enough to justify a ₹4.5-lakh-a-month rep, a 33% concession broke the logic of hiring outbound reps at all. The lesson: outbound's economics were more sensitive to sales discipline holding under pressure, inbound's to a single traffic source not disappearing. Both were fragile, in different places.

5. Nuances a learner must sit with

Intent is the real variable, not the channel

Devika's predecessor had treated "inbound" as a synonym for content marketing and "outbound" as a synonym for cold calling. They are adjacent, not identical. A paid search ad triggered by a buyer's own search is outbound spend riding on inbound intent — the buyer moved first, the seller paid to be visible. An unprompted referral from an existing customer is inbound with zero content involved. What separates the two motions is whether the buyer's need surfaced before the seller's message arrived. Get this backwards and a team labels its paid demand-generation "inbound" and wonders why its economics do not behave like organic content.

Inbound is not free; it is pre-paid

Outbound cost is visible and immediate — a rep's salary, a data subscription — which makes it look expensive next to a blog post. But the ₹27 lakh Tantuka's content team costs every quarter is a sunk, ongoing bet; the programme's first eighteen months produced almost nothing bookable. Comparing this quarter's inbound spend to this quarter's outbound spend, as Devika's first draft did, understates inbound's true cost by ignoring the unprofitable years behind today's ranking.

Outbound needs a defensible list; inbound needs a defensible keyword

Outbound quality collapses if the target list is wrong — sharp emails to the wrong eleven hundred companies produce the same zero as sloppy emails to the right ones. Inbound quality collapses if the chosen keyword has no real search volume, or is a term a larger competitor already owns. Each motion has one upstream decision that, if wrong, makes everything downstream irrelevant.

Sales-cycle length is a leading indicator, not a lagging one

A prospect who arrives inbound has usually done some of their own education, which shortens the cycle; one reached outbound often needs the category explained first, which lengthens it. Teams measuring "cost per lead" without tracking cycle length by source overrate outbound's apparent cheapness, since a longer cycle ties up a rep's time no cost-per-lead figure captures.

What it cannot tell you: whether the market exists at all

Neither motion answers whether enough manufacturers have the problem Tantuka solves, at a price they will pay. Traffic volume and reply rates are both downstream measurements of demand that already exists; reading either as proof of market size, rather than as evidence about which channel best reaches a market of unknown size, is a conclusion the data cannot support.

Blend once you know which motion is priming which

The common error past novice stage is treating the two as permanently separate budgets rather than noticing they compound: an outbound rep who mentions "you may have seen our export-documentation guide" gets a warmer reply, because the prospect's guard is already down. Mature teams route outbound at prospects who visited the site but did not convert, letting inbound narrow the outbound list rather than running blind.

Questions to ask before relying on either

Does our buyer already know they have this problem, or must we teach them it exists first? Is there a search term or community where they already look for answers? How long would content take to compound versus a rep to ramp? And what does our existing customer base's origin story reveal about which motion has already worked, even by accident?

6. How this differs by product and by company stage

In consumer products, inbound usually means app-store search, word of mouth and influencer curiosity rather than search-engine content, since the buyer's research is shorter and more social; a meditation app like Bandhani grew almost entirely on inbound in its first two years — app-store search-term work plus Instagram creators who used it unprompted — because cold-calling a person about a meditation app does not scale. In B2B the sales cycle and contract value are large enough that outbound's cost per touch is easier to justify, which is Tantuka's situation. In marketplace products the calculus splits by side: a trucking marketplace like Karigar Freight must push outbound on the supply side, calling truck owners with no reason to search for it, while relying on inbound for shippers who already search "reliable trucking Chennai to Coimbatore." Treating both sides the same way is a frequent early mistake.

Stage matters as much as category. An early-stage company rarely has the content history for inbound to produce volume quickly, so many lean outbound by necessity even where their buyer would, in principle, respond well to content — there is no eighteen-month runway to let a content engine compound. An established company inherits years of search authority a smaller competitor cannot replicate, which is why Devika's comparison, run on an eighteen-month-old programme, likely understated what year-four inbound economics would look like.

7. Common mistakes

The first mistake is running outbound with no ideal customer profile narrower than "manufacturing companies": reps burn through the list at a reply rate under 1% and sales blames the product. The misunderstanding is treating volume as a substitute for targeting; the cheapest diagnostic is asking a rep to name the last five accounts contacted and why each specifically needed the product — vague answers confirm the list is too broad.

The second mistake is measuring inbound purely on traffic rather than qualified pipeline: marketing celebrates doubled visitors while sales has no leads worth calling. The misunderstanding is conflating attention with intent; the diagnostic is checking what fraction of new traffic lands on a page with no path to a demo request — if it is most of it, the growth is vanity.

The third mistake is abandoning a channel after one bad quarter without separating a structural problem from a ramp problem: a team kills outbound after new hires miss quota in month one. The misunderstanding is expecting reps to perform at steady state immediately, when ramp curves of three to six months are typical; the diagnostic is checking whether reps who missed quota are also below expected activity volume — if activity is on target and results lag anyway, that is a targeting problem, not a ramp problem.

The fourth mistake is letting outbound volume erode the brand inbound depends on: prospects on inbound-sourced calls mention being annoyed by unrelated cold emails from the same company. The misunderstanding is running the two motions as separate teams with no shared view of who has been contacted; the diagnostic is checking whether sales and marketing share one contact database or two.

8. What good looks like

Two years before Devika's decision, a founder named Rohan Bhide had faced a similar fork at Chanderi Cloud, a compliance-automation vendor selling to hospital administrators. He did not treat it as either-or. He spent nine months almost entirely on inbound — three researched guides on an accreditation requirement hospitals were struggling with, distributed through hospital-administrator associations rather than paid search, since his buyer trusted those associations more than Google. That produced only eleven customers, but something more valuable: clear evidence of which three sentences made an administrator lean in during a call. He then hired two outbound reps, not six, and gave them those sentences as the opening of every cold email, targeted at two hundred hospitals sharing the same accreditation deadline — a real, dated trigger, not a guess. Reply rates ran near 9%, roughly four times the industry rule of thumb, because the message was not cold in substance even though the recipient was cold in relationship. Chanderi's outbound worked because its inbound phase had already told it what to say and to whom.

9. What Devika decided

Devika funded neither original proposal in full. She kept the content programme at half its requested budget, protecting the one asset that had already proven itself — the export-documentation guide's search ranking — and redirected the rest toward two outbound account executives rather than six, with an explicit rule: their target list would be built from companies that had already visited Tantuka's website without converting, plus a smaller set of net-new manufacturers matching her seven best existing customers. Tantuka lacked Chanderi's outbound message proven on inbound-warmed prospects first, but had enough inbound signal to narrow the list, worth more than doubling headcount and hoping. She told the board she expected to fall short of the sixty-account target from this lever alone, and that the shortfall was the honest number, not one to be closed by adding untested reps in month one.

What Devika needs to learn next is the topic this one unlocks: once both motions are running, which one earns the next incremental rupee of budget — a question about marginal returns this topic, concerned only with the initial choice of direction, does not yet equip her to answer. Two questions worth sitting with: if your best customer today arrived by accident of timing rather than deliberate channel choice, what does that tell you about which motion to formalise first? And if you could measure only one number before deciding between inbound and outbound, would it be cost per customer, or how much of the buyer's education your channel had completed before your salesperson ever spoke to them?

Case: Dropbox — The Fence, the Loop and the Pro Decision

Freemium and referral virality are usually taught as two growth tactics Dropbox happened to run at once. They are not separate: they are two instruments denominated in the same currency, pointed in opposite directions.

1. Two rooms, two decisions

On 6 February 2026, in a converted textile godown off Bannerghatta Road in Bengaluru, Nandita Bhattacharya opened a spreadsheet she had been avoiding. She was head of product at Deodhi Labs, whose product read a team's pull requests and wrote the first draft of the code review: 41,000 developers on a waitlist, 2,800 on a hand-approved free tier, 310 paying seats at ₹1,850 a month. The board wanted the Dropbox move — open the tier to everyone, pay developers in free usage for inviting teammates, let the loop do what a four-person sales team could not.

The spreadsheet said something inconvenient. Deodhi's free tier cost ₹41 per active free user per month in inference, and the average did not hold still: the most engaged decile cost ₹290, and on every cohort chart those were the users most likely to convert. The Dropbox analogy assumed a free tier's cost is a thin film over a vast dormant base; Deodhi's was concentrated precisely where its revenue was. "If we open the gate," she wrote, "our COGS scales with the thing we are trying to cause."

Eleven days later, in a first-floor office in Guindy, Chennai, Rajeev Menon ran the same debate in mirror image. His company, Gopuram Access Systems, made the video door-controller bolted to the gate of about 4,100 apartment complexes across six Indian cities, plus the resident app. Hardware sold to the resident welfare association at ₹6.4 lakh per gate and a 22% margin; the app was free. Gopuram had 1.9 million resident accounts and no consumer revenue.

Menon's proposal for the 24 February board meeting was Gopuram Pro: ₹99 a month for visitor history beyond seven days, recorded clips and multi-flat management for landlords. His head of sales objected that the association, not the resident, was the customer, and that a consumer subscription would confuse a procurement conversation already running nine months. His growth lead objected the other way: the 1.9 million accounts were the most valuable asset the company owned, and residents earning free months for getting their association to request a quote would start that cycle warm. Both were correct; neither told Menon what to do.

2. The idea, precisely, and who disagrees about it

Freemium is a pricing architecture in which a permanent, unexpiring, genuinely useful version of a product is given to everyone, and a paid version sold across a boundary — a fence — drawn on some dimension of use. The word was coined in March 2006 in the comments of Fred Wilson's "My Favorite Business Model," by Jarid Lukin; the practice goes back to the shareware authors of the early 1980s.

The economics were named before the word was. In Information Rules (1998) Shapiro and Varian argued that goods with near-zero marginal cost should be sold by versioning: differentiated variants that let buyers sort themselves by willingness to pay. Deneckere and McAfee put it more sharply in "Damaged Goods" (1996) — it can be rational to manufacture an inferior variant at a higher cost than the good one, purely to enable price discrimination. Freemium is second-degree price discrimination with the damaged version priced at zero.

The other half of the story has a separate lineage. The viral coefficient is epidemiology's R₀ borrowed for software — the Galton–Watson branching process of 1873, restated as k = i × c, where i is invitations per user and c the fraction that become users. Penenberg's Viral Loop (2009) popularised it; Ries canonised "viral" as one of three engines of growth. The lineages sit uneasily together, and four schools separate best by the exact proposition each would sign.

Nandita Bhattacharya's spreadsheet is that objection with a rupee sign on it.

3. Mechanics: three ledgers, one currency

Expert practice keeps three ledgers: growth (k, cycle time, amplification), cost (what a free user costs per month, and for how many months) and fence (where the paywall sits and how fast a user approaches it). Competent practitioners keep the first two. The expert sees that at Dropbox all three were denominated in gigabytes, which made the loop and the paywall one instrument pointed in opposite directions.

Recovering k from the outside

Instrumented viral coefficients are almost always overstated, because attribution credits the loop with signups it did not cause. A cleaner estimate comes from the steady-state identity: if signups in a period are N, of which Nr arrive by referral, and each user generates k referred signups, then Nr = kN — k is simply the referral share of signups, and amplification, the users eventually produced per non-referred signup, is 1/(1 − k). Drew Houston reported that the programme drove about 35% of daily signups, and separately that it had permanently increased signups by roughly 60%. Set k = 0.35: amplification is 1.54, a 54% uplift. Set the uplift at 60%: 1/(1 − k) = 1.60 implies k = 0.375. The two figures agree within two points. That is a real k — an order of magnitude above the 0.08 a naive invite count suggests — because it captures referred users referring in turn, which the single-generation calculation discards.

Cycle time governs survival, not size

With k below 1 the loop is a convergent series whose total is fixed by k alone. Cycle time T — the interval between a user joining and their referrals joining — does not change that total; it changes whether the total is ever banked. Amplification arrives generation by generation, (1 − kn+1)/(1 − k) after n of them, so 96% lands within three cycles. At T of four months the loop finishes inside a year; at fourteen months, roughly what a storage-triggered prompt produced, the third generation arrives three and a half years later, by which time 2% monthly churn has removed more users than the loop delivered. The test is not "is k above 1" but "is k/T greater than monthly churn."

The fence is a moving object

Dropbox's free tier was 2 GB; a user filling storage at 100 MB a month meets the wall in month twenty. Every referral pushed that wall away — 500 MB per side, capped at 16 GB for free accounts, with Pro accounts earning 1 GB per referral up to 32 GB. The asymmetry is the tell: Dropbox paid its paying users twice as generously, backwards if referral is an acquisition instrument and exactly right once you see what the bonus does to a free user.

This is the central mechanic and the step nearly every retelling leaves implicit. The programme was self-funding in cash — it cost disk, not bounties — but not in monetisation terms: it spent the same resource the paywall was made of. Dropbox took the trade because a referred user at $7–15 of effective acquisition cost, against paid search at $233 to $388, was worth a deferred conversion on the referrer's side, and because a richer bonus to Pro users defers nothing. The asymmetry is not generosity; it is the company declining to bribe its own prospects into never buying.

Choosing the fence dimension

The Pro decision is a versioning decision, and experts test a candidate fence against five criteria: monotone in value; observable and enforceable; growing with use, so it walks toward the user rather than being stepped over once; correlated with ability to pay; and ideally decoupled from the reward currency. Storage satisfies four and fails the last — the tension of Figure 1 — while a feature checklist fails the third outright. Hence Pro at $9.99 for 50 GB, with the ceiling twenty-five times the free one rather than three: the boundary had to read as relief, not a nudge.

4. When it applies — the claims to test

The conditions under which the Dropbox architecture works can be stated as claims that are true or false of a given business — and both protagonists fail different ones. A sixth holds for both: free users improve the paid product, through Deodhi's accepted-suggestion data and through resident adoption, Gopuram's best predictor of renewal.
